of the issues involved in the decisions affecting riding boundaries in that particular province. When we talk about using the wisdom and experience of parliament to apply to a particular situation I think in fairness, sir, and in the interests of accuracy it should be said that that type of knowledge goes very little beyond the borders of the particular province involved. At any rate that has been my observation.
Now, sir, you have indicated by your ruling this morning that you do not intend to permit discussion of the boundaries of particular ridings and I shall certainly respect your ruling, Mr. Speaker; but I ask whether a system can be defended in principle which results in glaring inequalities, inequalities of population as between constituencies in the same province, in the same part of the same province-for instance a low of 30,000 compared to 90.000 on the other hand. That cannot be justified in principle, Mr. Speaker, and it is principle that, as I understand it, we are discussing in this particular debate. When we see cabinet ministers enjoying benefits of ridings with low populations, pocket boroughs of which the sitting members are cabinet ministers, then again, sir, I think that is a situation that cannot stand up to honest and fair criticism.
So much, sir, for the system currently in vogue. I have had to speak critically of it because I speak of it as I have found it and as I have seen it, but I would like to speak briefly now of the other alternative, the proposal for dealing with this matter by a commission.
As I indicated earlier, I came to the view I now hold after having entertained originally -and when I say "originally" I mean in previous years-some serious doubts on the subject. I was impressed by arguments to the effect that this was a matter in which parliament itself should retain complete responsibility. However, Mr. Speaker, in the light of what I have now seen I am satisfied that another and better method must be found. The method by commission in the light of experience with such a method in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa has so much to commend it that I think in all earnestness it ought to receive a fair and complete trial here in Ottawa. It is true, sir, that in the United Kingdom this method has worked with eminent satisfaction. There is no responsible quarter in the United Kingdom today, as I am informed, from which criticism is directed at the commission method of achieving redistribution. If it can be made to work with such general satisfaction in the

Redistribution
United Kingdom I do not see why, Mr. Speaker, this parliament cannot put it to work with equal satisfaction.
Now, sir, I wish to deal frankly with this question of whether the commission method does subtract something from parliament's control. In the United Kingdom there is a good deal of vigilance on the subject of retention of parliamentary control. That experience gives me reason to think that there is no basic discrepancy between the application of this method and the maintenance of parliamentary control, which is a very important factor for those of us who sit in the official opposition. But does it mean that there is a contradiction, Mr. Speaker? I think not. When the report of the commission is completed it still requires a statute of parliament to give the formal effect of law to that report, and there will then be in parliament the fullest opportunity for discussion of the report of the commission. The experience and knowledge of members of parliament will be available to be brought to bear on such report. There is no reason to think there will not be the fullest opportunity to discuss such report and when the report comes before this house, as a report is going to come before this house from its committee on redistribution either tonight or Monday, Mr. Speaker, the result will depend in large measure upon the weight behind the report. When the house receives the report of the commission it knows at any rate that the commission, if it is an adequate commission, has carried out its task and made its report without any desire to sharpen political axes, to liquidate political opponents or to perpetrate hardships and injustices upon individual members of this house or members of the party that happens to be in a minority.
The report of a commission if it came to parliament would I think receive the respect that would be due to the commission having regard to the personnel of the commission, the thoroughness of its labours and the intrinsic merits of its report. Parliament then will have full opportunity of weighing that report and taking its responsibility for either enacting that report and its recommendations into law or on the other hand for differing or departing from the recommendations made by a commission appointed with the consent of parliament.
Now, sir, there is another feature to this method of appointing a commission which must be faced. If there is to be a commission that body will require guidance from parliament as to the principles which it should follow in proceeding with its task. Now, there
fMr. Fleming.]
are some principles that are discussed from time to time; there are principles to which lip service is given here and elsewhere from time to time. But so far as I am aware, Mr. Speaker, there has been no attempt by this house to write principles in the form of law or in any form that would, even be binding upon a committee of this house, with the inevitable result that when a committee is appointed it has virtually a free hand to apply a principle, disregard a principle, or to apply a principle in one case and to ignore it in another case.
Mr. Speaker, with a commission appointed under parliamentary authority I think parliament will be obliged to take responsibility for directing that commission as to the principles which it ought to follow. In this house there have been proposals by one or two members indicating principles. There would have to be a body of principles. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has made a useful contribution with the suggestion on his part that the following would be principles worthy of parliamentary adoption for the guidance of any commission appointed to carry out redistribution:
(a)	permanence in the definition of the boundaries of electoral districts is desirable;
(b)	the development of a sense of community of interest among the electors in each electoral district is to be encouraged;
(c)	the territorial area included In each electoral district should be continuous;
(d)	electoral district boundaries should follow the lines of division between recognized municipal, administrative or other areas by reference to which the census figures have been compiled;
(e)	the population included in each urban electoral district should be greater than in each rural electoral district;
(f)	the population of each urban electoral district in any province should be equal, and that of each rural electoral district in each province should likewise be so.
It may not be, in every case, simple and easy to apply all such principles, but at any rate they would be a useful guide. There are others that could be added to them. I do not suggest that such a list is necessarily exhaustive, and I do not suggest that it is complete. But at any rate, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to have a fair and comprehensive discharge of the duty of redistribution unless there is some attempt to lay down principles in a way that will be binding upon those who are charged with carrying out the task of redistribution. As long as we follow the method of a parliamentary committee, I cannot see that we are going to have anything but the kind of situation we have now, where the principle is applied where it happens to suit the majority and disregarded where it happens not to suit their purpose.

Then there is a third aspect of this matter of the commission method, and in my view it is vital. The success of the commission method depends upon the quality of the personnel of the commission. We would not be very much further ahead if the government simply exercised the power it enjoys at the hands of the majority of this house and appointed a commission of partisans of its own choosing; that is not the kind of commission for which the leader of the opposition is contending. It will have to be a commission composed of men whose objectivity in these matters is above suspicion. Remove the political motives that necessarily enter into the calculations of members of a parliamentary committee, and I think you will have gone a long way toward eliminating the injustices, the political liquidations that necessarily result under the present method.
The suggestion has been made by one or two members that the commission should be composed of judges. I do not wish to be taken as subscribing to that view, because I am not at all sure it is a proper position in which to put a judge. But I am satisfied, sir, that there are men in this country whose objectivity or sense of justice and fair dealing are beyond reproach, and who would be available to render what would be a very outstanding public service in such a capacity. They will have to be men with knowledge, and they will have to have assistance. I do not suppose there is anybody in this house, regardless of the length of time he has been in the house or the extent of his travels across this country, with all the knowledge the members of such a commission would require. The plan put forward by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has taken account of that fact, and proposed that assistance be provided by way of advisers or what he calls assessors in the various provinces, to assist those who are members of the commission appointed for this purpose.
Therefore I say that whatever objections have been raised to the commission method are capable of being fully met. There is no reason whatever why this method should subtract anything from the responsibility or the control of parliament over redistribution, or its duty in that regard. If the government of the day will apply its considerable ingenuity to the selection of men, and do it in consultation with the other parties in the house, there is no reason why competent men could not be appointed. The hon. member for Quebec South proposed that the political bias which would tempt the government in the naming of the personnel of such a committee be eliminated by having the 55704-247J
Redistribution
appointments made in consultation with the leader of the opposition, who it was proposed would also consult others in the opposition as well. I am satisfied, sir, that if there is a will on the part of the government to see redistribution carried out in such a way that it will accomplish and not defeat justice, that will really be a fair, comprehensive and principled redistribution, it can be done by this commission method. It is not being done, and I am convinced it cannot be done under the method currently in vogue.
There is a question of the time element as applied to the present situation. As the leader of the opposition pointed out this morning, if we were about to prorogue in a day or two it might be said that by advocating the reference of this matter at this stage to a competent commission it would inevitably result in delay. Even if it did result in delay, Mr. Speaker, until the next session, that would be a very small price indeed to pay for so desirable a purpose. I do not think we are likely to need the redistribution act before the next session of parliament. I do not think the government will be in great haste to call a general election before parliament meets again. I believe they have had their fingers sufficiently burned recently in a series of by-elections so that any fears or expectations that there will be a general election before another session of parliament can be eliminated. I believe the feeling that the redistribution bill will need to be carried into legislative effect before another session of parliament has been allayed.
If there are those who are in great haste to see this redistribution put into effect before the next regular session of parliament, then, as the leader of the opposition pointed out today, the method is ready. Let us provide now for the appointment of the commission to take this task in hand, and they can derive whatever value-and very doubtful it will be indeed-there may be from the report of the committee of this house on redistribution. Then when this parliament meets in the fall, still in the present session, the commission's report could be laid before the house. The house could deal with it before the prorogation of the present session.
My final word, sir, is this. What my leader had to say this morning about preserving public respect for parliament as an institution is entitled, it seems to me, to very weighty consideration by members in all parts of this house. The strength of our parliamentary institutions in this country is no greater than the respect people have for those who serve them in this place. If the impression continues to be borne in upon the minds of the public that parliament goes about the task

Redistribution
of redistribution simply by sharpening political axes and practising not the rules of fair play but the law of the jungle, then, Mr. Speaker, we are going to witness a continued decline in the respect of the public for their parliament. In days like these, when the battle for men's minds is a sharp battle being fought on a long front, let no one of us dare to turn his back upon his responsibility for seeing that the rules which govern the distribution of seats and which, in turn, determine in a large measure the representation of the people within this sovereign House of Commons, are governed by fair play. We should see that the procedure is carried out with justice, and is not calculated simply to pay off political debts or guided by political expediency at the expense of principles.
There are many imperfections, sir, in the way our parliamentary institutions function. We are all conscious of them, I think. Perhaps we in the opposition are more conscious of them than are those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, because we see more of the imperfections. But this is a human institution. Can hon. members leave the public any longer with the impression that the redistribution of seats in this house is determined simply by political expediency and the arbitrary exercise by the majority in these committees of the rights which they happen for the time being to possess as majorities? Times like these, Mr. Speaker, are much too serious for us to be any longer parties to the creation of an impression like that in the minds of the public.
In what I have had to say, sir, I hope I have been not unfair to people in different political parties. There is no member of any party who can go into that committee on redistribution and completely put aside party considerations or assume the role of objectivity which is rarely evidenced in this house or in our own political courses. We are here representing the people. We are here also as persons who subscribe to a particular party. What I have had to say, Mr. Speaker, by way of criticism of the way in which things are being done is not only criticism of the way in which the present majority in this house exercises its rights as a majority in the committee and the subcommittees, but is directed at a system where majorities, if the system continues, are always going to attempt to exercise their powers for the political benefit of the party to which they happen to be attached.
In times like these, Mr. Speaker, that kind of course is not good enough. Therefore I say that while I did not come to this decision quickly or lightly I am satisfied, on

the strength of an extremely unhappy and disappointing experience as a member of the committee on redistribution appointed by this house, that the present method can no longer be retained. It is no longer entitled to any respect on the part of the public or of this house. It is at best a piecemeal method. It is not a method that is based upon principle. It is a method that is based largely upon political expediency. I say the time has come to discard this method and at least give a fair trial to another method such as the alternative that has been found to work in an eminently satisfactory way in the United Kingdom and in our sister nations of the commonwealth.

Mr. Speaker, I think the necessity for a better means of redistribution than has existed in the past was amply shown by the proceedings of the past two or three months in the main committee on redistribution and in the subcommittees which have been working on this subject. I must say I speak from unfortunate personal experience when I say that.
I was a member of the committee this year for the first time, and I now realize how fortunate I was in not having been a member of the committee when the last redistribution took place. I think the present system can only be described as a mess. There was one remark by a Liberal member of the redistribution committee with which I think all members of the committee would heartily agree. He said, "Thank God this will not have to take place again for another ten years." I believe all hon. members who served on the committee were sick of the way the proceedings were carried out, and of the unsatisfactory results of trying to carry out a redistribution in this way.
On the other hand, the manner in which a commission such as has been suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) could operate was well illustrated by the work of the subcommittee which dealt with the Yukon-Mackenzie district. In other words that was an independent inquiry in which political considerations as well as personal desires, and a consideration of what might be to the advantage of an individual member, were absent. That procedure is bound to be more satisfactory than the present system of attempting to carry out a redistribution in which everyone is jockeying for position. Those factors-the absence of political considerations and personal desires-were absent so far as the subcommittee which dealt with the Yukon-Mackenzie district was concerned. No one on the subcommittee either represented or expected to represent either the Yukon or the Mackenzie area. There was no particular advantage to any party, no matter what was done. We realize that only one or two seats were involved, in any event. Circumstances were not such that anything in the nature of gerrymandering could be carried out.

In addition to that, the chief electoral officer was present at the committee meetings and gave expert advice as to the geography of the area and the problems involved in splitting it up, as well as in taking a vote. As a result of the absence of these factors there was a perfectly impartial discussion of the problem of redistribution in the Yukon-Mackenzie area, with the result that decisions were reached fairly and unanimously. I might add that to a large extent they were reached on the advice of the chief electoral officer. I would say that particular experience with redistribution might very well be taken to indicate how satisfactorily an independent commission could operate.

Being a member of the committee on redistribution this year was a very disappointing experience. Any idea a person might have had that redistribution would be carried out on a fair and impartial basis was dissipated very early in proceedings. It did not take long to get rid of that idea, if anyone had it at the beginning. The only principle that was apparent to me as far as redistribution went was the principle of political advantage. The various principles which were talked about were all contravened in one province or another or in one constituency or another. The principle stated to be followed in one particular province would quite often be the exact opposite to that which was being followed in the adjoining province. As has been indicated before, there should be some fixed and definite principle according to which redistribution will be carried out. These were outlined a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), and I shall mention just one.
I think the basic principle of representation is supposed to be and should be representation by population. That principle was fought for a hundred years ago and was thought to be firmly established in this country. Generally speaking this principle has been followed as far as the number of representatives in each province is concerned, though even in that regard there have been departures.

For example, in the case of the maritime provinces the special provision is that their representation shall not fall below the number of senators. This applies particularly to Prince Edward Island. I am not complaining about that, but it is a departure from the general principle. Then we have another departure in connection with Saskatchewan. Again I am not complaining particularly, but if we keep on departing from this general principle of representation we are soon going to have a situation where there will be no principle left in that regard.
It was away back in 1911, I think, that the exception as far as the maritimes were concerned, in favour of Prince Edward Island, was brought in. This year we have the exception in favour of Saskatchewan. If the present government has anything to do with the next redistribution and sees political advantage in it, I have no doubt another exception will be made. The first thing we know the whole principle will be gone.
When we come to the distribution of seats within the provinces we find that the principle of representation by population is honoured only in the breach. There just does not seem to be any regard paid to it in many cases. I think we should have some sort of provision in our electoral law, such as they have in Australia, where the size of a constituency cannot vary from the figure set- we will say it is 50,000 population-more than one-fifth up or down. I do not say that our provision should be one-fifth, but if we had a provision like that in this country we would avoid the extreme discrepancies which exist at the present time.
For example, in New Brunswick there is one constituency having just over 25,000 population and right next to it is another constituency with just over 84,000 population, or more than three and a half times as many people. The present redistribution has left them sitting exactly as they were; no change is to be made. Then when you come to deal with another province you hear the cry that a particular constituency cannot be left as it is because the population is too small. of the subcommittees was to have a certain amount of discussion and then the Liberal members of the subcommittee would bring in a plan prepared by a Liberal caucus or by the Liberal headquarters of the province concerned and the members of the subcommittee were practically told, "There it is". Following that there would be a long or short discussion. In the case of some subcommittees the discussion went on for weeks; in the case of other subcommittees it lasted only one or two meetings. But it did not matter whether there was a long or short discussion, it ended always with: "There is the plan".
Ordinarily the result was a deadlock of opposition members versus Liberal members. Then the chairman of the main committee, the minister, or the deputy chairman, the hon. member for St. Boniface, was brought in to act as chairman of the subcommittee and break the tie, as it were. That is when the axe fell. As far as I know the vote was always in favour of what the Liberal majority of the subcommittee had laid down as the plan. As far qs I can find out there was no disposition to make what might be called reasonable concessions.
Then the report of the subcommittee was presented to the main committee. In the main committee opposition members would move amendments to carry out the proposals they had made in the subcommittee. But the result was always the same. It did not matter what good arguments were presented, the decision of the Liberal members was always the same. As I have said, the arguments they used were the exact opposite of the ones that had been used in the subcommittee which had just reported, but the majority of the members of the main committee coming from other provinces would pay no attention to the arguments because they knew the way they were going to vote before they came into the committee. They may have been using exactly the same argument the opposition members used as far as another province was concerned, but they would just stand up and vote as a phalanx in favour of what the Liberal members from that particular province recommended.
In other words the thing did not work in a democratic fashion. I do not think there is any question but that the present procedure is not fair. I do not believe the people of Canada relish having this important matter of redistribution dealt with in the way it has been dealt with and is being dealt with. I think the people of Canada would welcome the setting up of a commission such as is asked for in the motion moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I believe the

should like to make a few comments on this matter. In the first place I am glad that this morning my leader was quite frank in referring to the cynical remark of a former leader of this party, when he said he was not suggesting the present method was unsatisfactory because it would be used by one party in a way that another party would scorn to do. He made no pretence of that kind. He dealt with the thing on what he considered to be its merits. He quoted at length from a former Liberal prime minister of this country.
My own feeling is that the events of the last few weeks have pointed up the difficulties of this method in a way that I, for one, had not fully realized before. I have to confess that within the last few weeks I argued against the appointment of a commission. I said that the difficulties of creating a commission and giving it instruction would be almost insuperable. I made that argument, and I am not denying that I think the difficulties will be very great. The only reason I am voting for this amendment-I hope the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) will not rise to a point of privilege when I say this-is that I have been through somewhat the same mental processes which he described himself as going through. I have felt, from all I could see of the operations of the present system, that it was so unsatisfactory that we should try something else.
It is not as if something else was not being tried elsewhere. Apparently it has been tried elsewhere, and with considerable success. I was not a member of the committee, which in one way is a great disadvantage and in another way is an advantage, because while I will not go the length of saying I speak non-politically-I do not know that any man is ever sure when he is speaking non-politically-nevertheless I have not had the overwhelmingly sense of frustration which has been experienced by some of the members of the committee.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) pointed out, very fairly I thought, that we in this parliament work on the basis that there is a government majority on committees; that is the practice. I do not see how we can complain about it; nevertheless it obviously does produce certain results.
[Mr. Rooney. 1
Here we have a situation, whether we like it or not, where we really have 262 members of parliament each with a vested interest, or hoping to have a vested interest, in a constituency. I think the difficulty of dealing with the thing impartially under such conditions becomes almost insuperable.
I do not know how they manage it in England, but apparently there is some tradition they follow which enables them to have committees which are not government-controlled. In the reports of the British parliament for 1948, during a debate on the representation bill, I find that Mr. Churchill referred to an incident which happened in 1944. I read it only to point out the difference, and to show that if that sort of thing could happen here we might not be facing the difficulty we are facing today. It does not happen here, however, and we might as well be honest with ourselves and say that it will not happen here. This is what he says referring to a committee discussing representation in 1944:
Although the Conservatives at that time had a majority of 150 over all parties in this house, the representation which we agreed to on the Speaker's conference

By the way, Mr. Speaker, apparently in Britain the Speaker presides over these conferences.
-was in a very different proportion. There were 15 Conservatives and 11 Socialists out of a total of 32, and when the Liberals and the few Independents were added, the Conservatives did not even have a majority on the conference, although they had a majority in the house of 150 over all parties. It was not dealt with entirely on the basis of House of Commons majorities.
I say that if we were prepared to do that sort of thing, then this situation might not arise. But we do not do it, and I think we should be honest with ourselves and admit that we do not do it. There is no sign that we will do it.
I feel that in the last few weeks, even since we failed to approve the motion of June 12, the situation has changed. It has, so to speak, sharpened. I have not been on the committee but, I am sure like every other hon. member, I have had indications every day of the difficulties which were being met, the sense of frustration and, what was worst of all, the feeling that in the end there was not going to be anything which could commend itself as fair. It would be just a bunch of bits and pieces. It would be the result of horse trading. When I say that I do not wish to suggest that this is a slur on anyone. As I said, we have 262 people with vested interests, and it is horse trading.
Again I revert to the suggestion of a commission. It would be extremely difficult. We

cannot just give them the population of Canada and ask them to divide it by 262 because, as I say, we recognize that there are other bases. I remember years ago reading a speech by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in which he argued that we had to have regard not only to the extent of the territory- which certainly has a practical bearing-but also that the existing political associations, like counties and so on, should be respected in so far as it is practically possible. Therefore I am not for one moment suggesting that this matter of redistribution will be an easy thing. I am only putting the suggestion forward, as the hon. member for Eglinton said, because I feel that anything will be better than what we are doing now; or at any rate I should like to try it to see if it is not better.
In passing I might say that I hope we shall not have to have recourse to the judges. Mr. Hackett, who sat in the last parliament, constantly harped on that point and I always thought he was right. He asserted that the judges should be kept as far as possible out of anything which might have a political aspect because such an association would tend to lessen that remoteness and impartiality which we so much desire them not only to have but to appear to have.
This point also occurs to me, Mr. Speaker. There are some men who are facing the elimination, or virtual elimination, of their constituencies. I myself had some small experience of that kind of thing five years ago, and I can understand what it means to a man who has represented a constituency for perhaps three or four parliaments to find that it is disappearing under his feet. Situations no doubt will arise where that has to take place. If it takes place as the result of a recommendation of a commission which the member feels has tried to look at the thing fairly, that is one thing; and he will just have to grin and bear it. But if in fact he has no such feeling; if in fact he looks about and sees that his constituency is eliminated whereas others have been left which look almost like pocket boroughs and which have populations less than his own, it seems to me it is utterly impossible for him to feel that he has been treated in a fair manner. I therefore come back, Mr. Speaker, and say that it seems to me the present situation is so unsatisfactory, so incapable of achieving a measure of fairness which will be respected by all concerned, that we should no longer continue with but should rather seek another method and at least give it a fair trial.

Mr. Speaker, the extent of the argument that
Redistribution
might be advanced on an occasion like this has been limited by the ruling made by the Speaker; and all I propose to do on this occasion is deal in some detail with the recommendations made by the leader of the opposition with reference to the setting up of a commission to determine this vexed question of redistribution that comes to the House of Commons for decision every ten years.
On this occasion I am not going into any detail in reference to any constituency. I am going to confine myself entirely to a discussion of the merits of and the need for a commission to determine this matter. I shall also deal in particular with some of those countries which have adopted this system and have found it to be both efficacious and nonpolitical.
I commence by reading the amendment, which is as follows:
. . . that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the enactment of a measure to provide for the appointment of a commission to effect the redistribution of electoral ridings in accordance with the census of 1951 and pursuant to the provisions of the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1952 inclusive; such commission to be instructed to make its report to this session of parliament upon the resumption of its sitting.
As the leader of the opposition pointed out, there is no difficulty in the way of adopting this suggestion at this time, for the reason that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has introduced, and this house has passed, a motion to the effect that the sittings of the house will be adjourned' until November. In anything the Prime Minister said in the course of his remarks there was certainly no indication of the possibility, much less the probability, of an election being called within the next three or four months. Indeed, all editorial writers have been unanimous to date in their opinion that the meaning of the Prime Minister's statement yesterday was that no election is in the offing and that, in any event, there would be none before the months following the coronation. The fact that the Prime Minister moved that motion gives added weight and importance to the proposition advanced by the leader of the opposition this morning, when he set forth the benefits of removing once and for all from the cockpit of partisanship the determination of a matter which is not directly the concern of members of parliament but is particularly that of the Canadian people.
I commence by saying that I am not one of those who believe that anyone has rights to any constituency. I believe that the changing events, the movements of population and the alteration in economic development all require a change from time to time in the

Redistribution
determination of the boundaries of constituencies. We in Saskatchewan-and this applies also to Manitoba-find ourselves in a different position from that of other provinces by reason of the amendment to the British North America Act, which was passed, by virtue of which Saskatchewan, instead of losing five seats, will lose three. In other words, in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba the basis of population will be different in the determination of constituency lines from that in any other provinces in the dominion affected directly by population considerations.
I know one can read the story of parliament and its actions through the years with regard to redistribution. Every ten years there is a recurring and ever-stronger feeling of resentment against the use, by abuse, of the power given to the House of Commons to determine the areas and the territorial limits of constituencies. I have read the debates through the years, and in each ten-year period the feeling has become stronger and stronger. I go back no further than 1932; and I do not believe any party-and that applies as well to my hon. friends of the C.C.F.-can wrap itself in the garb of political piety when it comes to looking at the question of redistribution. For in the province of Saskatchewan there was a redistribution within the last year or a year and a half that in several constituencies violated the principle of fairness that should have been in effect. I say that not by way of criticism but simply to accentuate my view that the time has come for parliament to determine whether or not we shall forever retain in parliament the power to determine boundaries.
The only reason we would want to retain it would be the political advantage of the party with the majority at the time. After all, the setting up of a commission will not remove from parliament the right and duty to determine the question once and for all. But, Mr. Speaker, the experience in Britain and elsewhere has been that when an independent commission speaks no parliament anywhere within this commonwealth has ever dared to alter the boundary lines of any constituency in a way which would have the result of liquidating a political opponent. In other words the commission system would provide a scientific means whereby redistribution would be determined on the only basis on which it should be determined, namely the question of population, subject of course in every case to these peculiar exigencies that occur in various constituencies where, by reason of the industrialization, the urban nature of a constituency, the rural nature of another, there has been

recognized at all times the' principle that population shall not be equal in all constituencies.
Having said that, I am going to make this one reference to the subcommittee for the province of Saskatchewan. It is going to be entirely objective, because I am not going to
discuss in any way any of the problems peculiar to Saskatchewan. I point out this. The subcommittee was set up some five or six weeks ago.

I shall not quote further from that, because the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) quoted it. During the course of that debate in 1947 I brought to the attention of the house the position in the United Kingdom. I did so because I believed it deserved to be canvassed. I am not by any means wedded to the idea of a judicial tribunal, for I know the argument can be advanced-and I have been one who for years has advanced it- that in any matter that concerns political partisanship, or may even have a suspicion of political partisanship, the judiciary should be kept from it in order that their position may remain as inviolate as it is possible to have it.
But, of course, the question of the type of commission to be set up is not dealt with in

Redistribution
the amendment offered by the leader of the opposition. After all, that is for determination by the government of the day, and ratification by parliament of the stand taken by the cabinet after it has made a decision in this regard.
On that occasion I made reference to the British system, in these words:
I suggest this, and I do so only in passing because the Prime Minister in 1933 indicated that some method must be found whereby fairness will be achieved and the liquidation of political opponents prevented or denied. I suggest consideration of the Redistribution Act of the United Kingdom. It is a matter which might well come up. It cannot come up at this session, but it might be considered.
It will be recalled that in that year the redistribution measure came in within the last two days of the session. Then I continued: It is entitled the "House of Commons (Redistribution of Seats) Act, 1944". In the United Kingdom the matter of redistribution is under continuous review; a permanent boundary commission has been set up. There are several boundary commissions, one in England and one for the several other parts of the United Kingdom.
At that point the then hon. member for Davenport, who was such an authority on these matters, interrupted by saying, "There are four", following which I continued:
Yes. A report is made to the house from time to time. It is a continuing activity which, of course, would be different from the procedure here in Canada. Provision is made that-and I read from the act-
Then I read from the act to indicate the means whereby, by continuing the activity, the constituency picture within the United Kingdom would be changed, based on transitions in population and the like. I quoted from the act as follows:
A report of a boundary commission under this act showing the constituencies into which they recommend that any area should be divided shall state, as respects each constituency, the name by which they recommend that it should be known, and whether they recommend that it should be a parliamentary county or division of a parliamentary county or a parliamentary borough or division of a parliamentary borough.
Then I went on to point out that in no way would the setting up of a commission be an abdication of the responsibility of parliament, and went on to say:
Then the draft is approved by resolution of each house of parliament. That commission is one which is above partisanship. Parliament still rules; parliament still controls; but parliament would not act unfairly against a political opponent.
Then I referred to the personnel of the commission in the United Kingdom in charge of this responsibility in these words:
The commission for England consists of the chairman, the registrar general, the director general of the ordnance survey and two other members, one appointed by the secretary of state and the other by the minister of health; and no member
IMr. Diefenbaker.]
of the House of Commons or of either house of parliament of Northern Ireland is permitted to act on such committee.
In other words the British found that a judicial commission was not in keeping with the finer traditions of an inviolate, independent judiciary. In Great Britain in 1944 the system I have indicated was set up.
Similar commissions have been set up in other parts of the commonwealth for the determination of the distribution of constituencies. Canada, indeed, is the only one of the self-governing dominions within the British commonwealth that adheres to the present archaic system, which is dangerous in the extreme if applied by an overwhelming and aggressive majority. No other part of the commonwealth adheres to this system.
As the leader of the opposition said this morning, in a world where democracy is challenged changes must inevitably take place. The fact that in the 1860's, 70's, 80's and 90's this system was regarded as a means whereby political opponents could be removed, and the fact that it has continued since, is no reason for maintaining a system that is the very negation of democratic principles, namely the application of equity and fairness within statutory limitations as provided by law.
I am going to read from a report made in 1939, for which I sent out a while ago. This is a report made by a special committee on electoral matters, headed by Mr. C. E. Both-well, the then member for Swift Current, who was a very distinguished member of the bar and of parliament.
It reads:
Your committee was instructed by order of reference dated March 13, 1939, to study and report on "Methods used to effect a redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and in other countries, and to make suggestions to the house in connection therewith," but regrets that it has been unable to give this order of reference the consideration It merits, owing to the number of meetings necessarily devoted to consideration of suggested amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, the last of which meetings was held on the second instant.
That report was dated May 10, 1939. The report concludes:
Your committee therefore submits, without further comment, a statement of the methods employed in other countries, and the suggestions made, for the consideration of the house.
I have pointed out already that so effective was the study made by that committee that a' bill would have been introduced by the then prime minister, Mr. King, in order to remove this record of partisanship which for too long has been the lot of the House of Commons every ten years, or even oftener in so far as the western provinces are concerned.

I should like to refer for a moment to the various systems in effect in other parts of the commonwealth. I have already given the house a not very detailed but I think sufficient summation to indicate what the plan is in Great Britain. I should lie to refer now to the Australian system which is set out in more detail in the minutes of evidence attached to the report made by Mr. Bothwell to which I allude4 a few moments ago. Here is the system followed in Australia:
A distribution commission is set up. Each state returns the number of members of the House of Representatives to which it is entitled on a population basis, but subject to the provision that each original state shall be entitled to be represented by five members.
The representation of each state is determined after each decennial census, and at an intermediate intercensal period five years thereafter, in the following manner-
In each state a commission is set up composed of the surveyor general and the chief electoral officer, with a chairman nominated by the governor general. In making a distribution the commissioners are instructed to give consideration to community or diversity of interest, means of communication, physical features, existing boundaries of divisions and subdivisions and state electoral boundaries. Objections or suggestions in writing may be lodged with the commissioners at any time during the thirty days following advertisement in the Gazette. After the thirty days mentioned the commissioners are required to submit their report and the minister must lay the report before both houses of parliament. If both houses of parliament pass a resolution approving the distribution, a proclamation is issued declaring the names and boundaries of the divisions. That in general is the system in effect in the commonwealth of Australia.
In the case of New Zealand two commissions are set up to provide for periodical readjustment of representation, one for each island. Each commission is composed of five members. That of north island consists of the surveyor general, two commissioners of crown lands who are named by their title of office, and two members not being members of the public service or members of the general assembly, as the House of Representatives nominates from time to time. One of the five is a permanent commissioner. Again in that case certain regulations are followed. A report is made and within ten days thereof the governor general is required to submit the report to the House of Representatives to be dealt with.
In South Africa they have a judicial system under which three superior court judges determine the matter subject to regulations.
Redistribution Each individual state reapportions its constituencies and determines what the representation shall be on the basis of constitutional or statutory provisions.
I have referred to these systems in order to indicate my support of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition and because I feel that in the interests of equity and fairness and in order to preserve the highest principles of representation in a democratic assembly the time has come to do that which Mr. King would have done had war not come and to which throughout the years he gave undivided support. At that time he was supported by two great leaders of his party, the late Colonel Ralston and the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, both of whom joined with him in the House of Commons in proclaiming the need of forever placing in the pages of history the record of the past and determining that parliament should once and for all assure that the bickering and prejudice which undermine our democracy every ten years when this question comes up could well be removed from partisanship as it has not been throughout the entire period of our confederation.

41.	To provide for assistance to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories, $1,000,000.

As the representative of a constituency whose citizens are vitally interested in the production of cheese, I should like to say a few words on this item. The cheese industry has had a good deal of consideration during this session. I do not wish to deal at any length with the difficulties which face the producers. Our inability to sell cheese on the British market has been a great disappointment to our producers; and the curtailment of our outlet in the United States, through the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, has also contributed to the difficulty.
There was some good news yesterday. I read a press report which stated that the restrictions in the United States may be modified. We hope for some kind of beneficial effect on our industry. If every citizen of Canada would consume, on an average, one-half pound of cheese more than he has been consuming in the past the difficulty would be resolved immediately. Our cheese is the best in the world. We have improved our quality so that it is exceeded by none.
I should like to ask a question of the minister in connection with this estimate. I notice that two years ago the amount appropriated for this purpose was $1,400,000. Last year it was $1,100,000. This year I notice the estimate is $1 million. I should like to ask whether the reduction has been in the amount which was provided for assistance to encourage the improvement of cheese or the improvement of cheese factories.

The quantity of cheese is down considerably. The amount of cheese that was being produced a few years ago was approximately 125 million pounds. Last

year it was about 80 million pounds. Of course the amount of money paid out is less.

The hon. member for Perth mentioned reading a newspaper article dealing with this industry. There is something in the press this morning with regard to the Ontario government doing something about the 15 million pound surplus. I wonder if the minister knows anything about that.

I hesitate to make a report about it. It is really a provincial matter. It was dealt with in Toronto yesterday, I think, by Mr. Kennedy at a meeting with the cheese producers. My information, although it is more or less indirect, is that they were successful in getting rid of the cheese. I should not like to make that as a definite announcement, however, or even as an announcement at all.
Is it entirely the provincial government that is doing that, or is it in cooperation with the dominion?

It is entirely provincial, apart from this consideration; that they are organized under the federal co-operative act, which only means that we guarantee them against loss up to 80 per cent of the average price over the last three years. But all the transactions are carried on by the co-operative itself and largely under Ontario legislation.
Is it a one hundred per cent responsibility of the provincial government now to look after surplus farm products across the country?
It always has been their responsibility to look after them if they could sell them within the province; and cheese is largely sold within the province.

I have just one suggestion to make. Would it be possible for the Minister of Agriculture to persuade the Minister of National Health and Welfare to use some of the advertising which seems to be at his command to advertise cheese as one of the best and most healthful foods we can eat? We see a great deal of advertising by that department; and I know of nothing better on which to spend money than on something to get our own Canadian people to eat one of the most healthful foods produced.

Does that mean the hon. member for Leeds agrees with me that some of the present expenditures of the Department of National Health and Welfare are being wasted and could be much better spent in such ways as the hon. member has indicated?

Item agreed to.

42.	To provide assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment, $500,000.

What is the total amount that has been voted to date under this item? I notice it has been in the estimates for a number of years now. How long is it expected that it will take to replace this equipment?
The Quebec government is expecting it will take two or three years yet in order to complete the expenditures that are necessary to make the change.
What is the total of the payments that have been made under this item over the years? In what year did they start and what have been the amounts paid each year?
They started in 1940, and the amount has been $2,250,000; that is, our share of it is $2,250,000. We pay one-third.

I believe the minister told us back in 1949 that it started in 1936, carried on for a year or so, skipped the war period and then started again just after the war. There had been some money spent at that time.
I think that is right, that it was started before the war began.
Can we get the exact figures?
The exact figures are here. We shut it off just at the beginning of the war for a time, but it had been going on for a short period. This record here is from 1940, which is for the war period.
As I understand it, this item is for maple sugar equipment that was defective in some way.

Those who are familiar with the maple sugar industry will remember that we used to be accustomed to see rusty pails hanging on trees. Someone conceived the idea of covering them with something which prevented them from rusting. It was a sort of lead covering, and the effect of the sap standing in the pails at times resulted in lead being taken into the sap and eventually appearing in the syrup, constituting a form of lead poisoning that condemned the syrup. The syrup that came out of those utensils was utilized largely in the making of cigarettes. The Americans objected to the syrup being shipped into the United States for human consumption.
We entered into an arrangement prior to the war; I think it is probably correct to say that we started discussing it in 1936. We did not get down to making payments until

Supply-Agriculture
1939-40. Payments up to the present have totalled $2,250,000 so far as we are concerned. It is a three-way arrangement under which the province pays one-third, we pay one-third and the people who are interested in the equipment take care of the other one-third.
The minister says only $2,250,000 has been spent by the dominion government?
Yes, that is right.
A total of $2,250,000?
Which is a lot of money.
It is $8 million altogether.
One of your colleagues does not think it is a lot of money.
How much longer are you going to continue this?

The work is done by the Quebec government. We simply undertake to pay one-third of the cost and the Quebec government does the actual administration. They tell us it will take another two or three years, but I must admit to the committee that I think it has taken a long time now. We are not carrying on the administration; the Quebec government is, and we shall probably have to check up sooner or later as to whether we should continue.
Is the Ontario government taking advantage of it also?
No; it is only in Quebec.

Item agreed to.
43.	For assistance in construction of potato warehouses under terms and conditions to be approved by the governor in council, $50,000.
What is the principle upon which assistance is given under this item?

Those co-operative organizations which have set up storages for potatoes started first in Prince Edward Island, and it has been taken on in some of the other provinces. The provision was that the province, or at least the co-operative, pays up to 25 per cent of the cost of putting up the storage and the province and the federal government split the other part equally between them.

44.	Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $3,249,270.
What is the estimate of the damage to the P.F.R.A. dams in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan owing to flooding conditions this spring?
An order for return was brought down quite recently, or an answer to a question was given, I have forgotten which, showing the total amount, which is something over $300,000.
Are repairs to those dams being undertaken at the present time?
Oh, yes, it is under way, and I imagine in connection with some of them pretty well completed.

Can the minister give any
estimate of the damage that has been done to the surrounding country in the loss of farms and livestock?

We had an increase in our estimates, including the supplementaries, which amounts to about $500,000, in order to take care of the damage done around about and to make some improvements in the structures.
The point I want to make is this. Does this vote include any compensation to the people who had losses in that flood?
Well, it includes compensation in this way. We put some of the structures back in action that were on people's property and were destroyed.

I know the provincial government is making itself responsible for some portion of that cost. The dominion government is not working in co-operation with the provincial government on any scheme of that kind?

Well, we are working in co-operation in this sense. I understand the provincial government put an inspector in at Eastend, for example, to inspect the houses that had been damaged, and to report upon possible improvements, and I think possibly putting some money in it as well. The federal government has done a great deal of work in Eastend and elsewhere through that area in putting the streets back in condition and putting the lots around the people's houses back in condition, pumping water out of their basements and re-establishing the situation in general. That is of course one of the reasons for the expenditure of that extra amount of money.

Is any of the money in this item for P.F.R.A. work in connection with cuts in the Assiniboine river?
There is only $50,000 in the supplementary estimates.
Item No. 50 deals with the Assiniboine river, diking and cut-off.

Will the minister tell me whether consideration has been given to extending the benefits of P.F.R.A. north of the present line west of Lloydminster and extending as far north as the North Saskatchewan river? I asked this question during discussion of item No. 1.

Well, it is involved in the larger question that we were discussing yesterday, as to whether we are going to extend P.F.R.A. work outside the Palliser triangle. That has not been done up to now, and I do not know whether it will be given further consideration until we apply the decision to all Canada rather than just to that area.

I should like to follow the hon. member for Saskatoon with one further question. With regard to some of these big fires and so on that have occurred in various places in the country, the federal government has assumed some responsibility for rehabilitation and aid. What strikes me about this Eastend situation is that it resulted from the destruction of a government project, a dam. It seems to me there is some responsibility for compensation to individuals who have suffered losses as well as the town of Eastend and the surrounding territory because of the failure of a government project which caused the inundation of the town and the country around that town. I should like the minister to comment. The very fact that the department felt it should use its facilities to pump water out of basements, to repair the streets, to rebuild the lots around the houses and so on would indicate that the department at least felt that it had some responsibility. The point I am making is that it would appear to me that the responsibility is not recognized to the extent it should be to the individuals who have suffered. Has that been given consideration by the department and by the government?

Well, yes, it has been given consideration. I think I explained here on one previous occasion the fact that it was given consideration; but there is a difference of opinion as to whether building the dam that was erected and placing the storage there, and also placing the controls at Cypress lake, which is above that, resulted in making it more likely that there would have been damage, or less likely. There was a dam there before the government stepped in at all, of course. The Watson estate had irrigation carried on at Eastend before the government *took any part in it. Later on the government took that project over and enlarged it. Our engineers maintain that anything that was done there did not increase the damage that would have been done in any case this year.

There was a much greater flow of water in the stream this year than is usual. Damage would have been done in any case. I quite understand that one will never be able to settle that; there will always be arguments as between one group and another. We have equipment there which is working on irrigation all the time, in other words it is handling water. It is just a reasonable thing-it is not a matter of admitting anything at all- that when we have equipment there, and people's basements fill up, we pump them out. The fact is that we simply put the pumps to work, and pumped them out. That was the natural thing to do. However, it cost money to do it; and we require to have a vote to cover it.
The irrigation that was carried on there was not only in the country but was also done in respect of people's lots in the village itself. The water coming down through the village took some of the lots almost entirely away, at least it took away the top covering of earth. We used our equipment to put it back again. In some cases streets were torn up by the water, and we used our equipment in that connection, too. In other words, when we were putting in the ditches, the boxes, and all that sort of thing associated with irrigation, we completed the job in a way that was helpful to everyone.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think this item should be allowed to pass without some expression of appreciation for the splendid work the department is doing through the expenditure of this money. I have no doubt the great number of relatively small works throughout the prairie provinces are of benefit to agriculture out of all proportion to the amount of money invested in them.
I agree with that.

We in British Columbia do appreciate the minister's entry, through this branch of his department, into one or two relatively small projects, the largest of which was a river containment plan at Pemberton. The hon. member for Kamloops is not in his seat to thank the minister, so I shall do so. There is some work being done on the west bench at Penticton and some work at West-bank in the Okanagan.
I was wondering if that expenditure would come under this item, and if we in British Columbia are officially acknowledged as one of the areas for P.F.R.A. assistance. I am wondering if we may expect the minister's engineers to continue their investigations within British Columbia, because in that

Supply-Agriculture
province there are a number of additional points where this sort of help would be of great benefit to us.

The expenditures we are making in British Columbia would come under item 47 which deals with land protection and reclamation. However, it was as a result of the P.F.R.A. work we have done on the prairies that this work in British Columbia was undertaken some years ago. The first was in the Pemberton area, and it has been pretty well completed. I believe this season will complete what was undertaken there. There is the possibility of doing other work. We are undertaking further projects in the Okanagan valley and elsewhere, under this item.

I listened carefully to the minister's statement a few moments ago about Eastend. It must also be remembered that Medicine Hat suffered a serious flood this year. Whether it was occasioned by the going out of the Seven Persons dam, I cannot say. We know, however, that the spillway of the dam went out, and that the results were disastrous. If Medicine Hat is to be treated in the same way as Eastend, then Medicine Hat should be given some compensation for the damage caused through the going out of the spillway. Is it the policy of the government to give assistance in cases of this kind?

I should imagine the hon. member would know as much as anyone about the situation out there. My officials say they have not received a report about any serious damage at that point. We realize that there is damage, of course, in the event of a big run-off of water in the spring of the year.

As a result of the spillway of the Seven Persons dam going out, the city of Medicine Hat was flooded. Hundreds of families were kept out of their homes.
I am sure all hon. members will recall reading about it in the newspapers. Today we are still taking up subscriptions to assist in putting the lots back into proper condition, pumping out the basements and other work of that kind. Many of the homes are damaged beyond repair. Would the policy that applied to respect of Eastend also apply to Medicine Hat?

The Seven Persons dam is a small stock-watering dam. I can scarcely understand how it would do that much damage. However, we will check and find out whether it was the cause of the damage. I would imagine, however, that 
any damage for which we would be responsible would only be that having to do with the stock-watering end of it, at the dam itself.
Under which of these items is work being carried on at The Pas in northern Manitoba in connection with the raising of dikes and reclamation of land?
It would be under item 48.

Mr. Chairman, I rise at this time as a result of the comments made the other day by the minister in connection with the possibility of the provisions of P.F.R.A. being extended to other parts of Canada. As the minister and hon. members will know, in Ontario we have a number of persons engaged in conservation work. While this is in its earlier stages, public opinion is gradually being awakened to a realization of its importance. I feel sure I am voicing the sentiments of many farmers in Ontario when I say we would be deeply interested in having set up, perhaps under different auspices, a body similar to P.F.R.A. to take care of this problem in Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, the people in the area I represent deeply appreciate the help that has been given to them in the past through the construction of dugouts. A good deal of irrigation has been carried on from these dugouts through the use of sprinkler systems. A short time ago the board of trade of Hanna passed a resolution, of which I believe the minister was sent a copy, asking that a grant be made toward the purchase of a sprinkler system. I raised this matter I think three years ago. At that time some confusion was created in the minds of the people out there as to whether or not it was possible to get a grant under the P.F.R.A. for the purpose of purchasing a sprinkler outfit. The minister said that it was not, but I believe there was an understanding that if a farmer paid the full cost of building a dam or constructing a dugout it would be possible for him to get a grant from the government for the sprinkler system in lieu of the money that would have been paid on the dam. I do not know whether that is correct, but I think the minister will agree that it is a reasonable proposition. If a farmer has constructed a dam or paid the whole cost of constructing a dugout he should be able to get the amount of money he would have got from the government for that purpose.

It has not been our policy to assist in the purchase of sprinkler outfits. We do assist farmers to put in dugouts or dams. I suppose the dams the hon. member has in mind were put in before this policy was first in effect, which would be some

seventeen years ago. I doubt if since that time there have been many dugouts constructed for which assistance was not given. I would hesitate to go back seventeen years and start to give special assistance in connection with dams or dugouts constructed before that time.

Apparently the farmers were not aware that they could get grants and they went ahead and constructed the dams and then found that a grant could have been obtained. They were advised by the local agricultural authorities to use a sprinkler system, and they now wonder whether they can get money for that purpose when they did not ask for any assistance in the construction of the dams.

I do not think the government would want to adopt a plan of that kind. It would seem a considerable expenditure of money for something similar to a lot of other equipment on the farm with which we might be asked to help as well.

It seems to me that we are in a rather precarious position. The government builds a dam to store water; then when the dam goes out the government must compensate the people for building the dam. It looks like a kind of vicious circle. Where do the provinces enter into these rehabilitation and protection schemes?

The P.F.R.A. is handled by our own organization which spends the federal money. Personally I am a strong believer in the principle that the people who raise the money should spend it. In this particular case we raise the money and we spend it. I think we get better results that way. As far as a vicious circle is concerned, we probably do put back the dams when they go out. I suppose the principle is that they should have been put in well enough to stay there. We were talking about bridges earlier along somewhat the same lines. We have had no difficulty at all with by far the greater number that have been put in.

I want to say that we do appreciate what the P.F.R.A. has done in the way of water storage, but many times a good dam is constructed and then the spillway is left uncompleted. I suggest to the minister and his parliamentary assistant that when dams are put in the spillways should be completed. We have had several instances of this kind, and I mention the Ross creek irrigation project in particular. The P.F.R.A. and the Alberta government spent considerable money on that project. The material was all there but it was not completed, and will
Supply-Agriculture
now cost the dominion government about three or four times as much as it would in the first place.
Then the spillway was not completed in connection with the Eagle Butte dam. We were all afraid that dam would go out this year, but fortunately it did not. It seems to me that when the P.F.R.A. undertakes one of these projects the spillway should be completed, because that is very important in the storage of water. I do not mean this as criticism; I am simple offering advice and suggesting that these spillways should be completed so that what happened this year, last year and the year before cannot happen again.
I am glad to see that the department is spending some money in connection with water storage because we need water out there, especially in the summertime. But when a good dam is built, see that the spillway is completed so the dam will be protected when the spring run-off occurs.

I have been listening to the discussion, particularly that of the hon. member for Medicine Hat; and to a maritimer it would appear that when these dams are built, they are built by the P.F.R.A., and then when they do not work properly, it is still the fault of parliament. It would seem to me that it works both ways. If it works, it is the fault of parliament, and if it does not work, it is still the fault of parliament. P.F.R.A. then means parliament's fault regardless of action. It looks pretty hard to determine whether these projects should be undertaken.

I would point out to the hon. member that when a wharf is built in Nova Scotia and for some reason it is washed out, naturally they want it replaced. They holler their heads off if it is not replaced.

That is not the point. If the wharf is built and something around it is damaged, we would not expect the government to come back and repair it. Following your argument it would look as though after they were built it was still parliament's fault regardless of what happens.
I have listened with interest to the debate, but I would like to ask the minister who puts up the money if these dams require maintenance.
I wonder if the hon. member would speak louder.
If the others would keep quiet it would be all right.

I know that when these dams get into disrepair the farmers say, let it wash

It is perhaps trite to say that the people of Saskatchewan are very disappointed at the tardiness with which the dominion government is proceeding with the work on what is commonly called the South Saskatchewan dam. I think the right hon. minister must bear some of the responsibility for that disappointment, because he has constantly painted glowing pictures of what the dam would mean to the province of Saskatchewan. He has said it would create a great agricultural revolution in that province, and I think with that I can agree at this time. The fact is, however, that this project has been delayed beyond all expectation, and indeed beyond all reason.
As I said, the minister himself has created glowing pictures of what that dam will mean to us as security against drought. I am afraid that in many of his pre-election speeches particularly he has made unfulfilled promises and we are very disappointed at the delay. I will not go into the history of the project.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Lethbridge gave us a very interesting background of the story of that part of the country the other day, and the minister told him that when we got to this item he would be prepared to discuss it. I feel it is simply my duty to say that the people of Saskatoon, who are looking forward to the results of the building of this dam, if it is indeed ever built, would expect me to register the protests they have made. Representations of course are constantly made to me as their member. I have for instance in front of me a letter from the Saskatoon board of trade dated June 4, 1951, addressed to the Prime Minister expressing their desire in the matter and their disappointment that action has been delayed.
There is in that part of the country, as the minister well knows, an organization known as the Saskatchewan rivers development association, which is doing valuable publicity work in regard to the matter. They have an annual meeting, and I am well aware that annually at least they send the minister an expression of their desires. I have in my hand such an expression under date of June

15, 1951, in the form of a wire addressed to the Prime Minister. I think I should read this one:
Knowing that the irrigation of central Saskatchewan will raise the economic standards of our province to their proper place in our national economy and being assured that the South Saskatchewan river project is both feasible and practicable, we, the S.R.D.A. in annual meeting today, record our regret that the government has seen fit to delay approval of construction pending further consideration by a committee of experts; but in view of this decision we strongly urge the government to make this selection of experts without delay and that they be requested to hasten their report in order that an approval of the project may be entertained by the government at the coming fall session. So urgent is the need we ask that the project be proceeded with immediately.
I would also like to quote from the newspaper in our city, which certainly cannot be accused of doing anything but supporting this government and its kindred Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan. I may say that is particularly true before elections; and if the minister read, as I have no doubt he did, the copies of the Star-Phoenix for the month previous to the recent provincial elections I think he will bear me out in that regard. I have not criticized the minister very severely, nor indeed the government, but this paper is more severe in its criticism. The article or editorial is entitled "No argument". It is contained in the June 2nd Star-Phoenix and it says among other things:
The federal government's decision to pigeonhole the South Saskatchewan dam project is only less amazing than Mr. Gardiner's reasons for doing so. The project has been studied, surveyed, analysed, discussed and debated for more than four years.
I think that is an understatement, because I heard the minister, as I have reminded him before, make a very eloquent speech at the technical school in Saskatoon in 1944 in which he promised untold millions for the construction of water projects in the province of Saskatchewan.
The only part that is wrong is your last statement.

The article continues:
On June 24, 1950, Mr. Gardiner assured an audience at Outlook that "I can tell you tonight that we know, that our engineers are satisfied the dam is feasible." He intimated that an arrangement between Ottawa and the provincial government for sharing the cost was the only thing then holding up a start on the project.
That is a very Gardiner-like statement.
That arrangement has since been made. And now Mr. Gardiner says more experts are to be called in to study, survey, analyse and debate, because, he implies, some of his colleagues in the government are still doubtful. Has the government lost confidence in its own engineers, we wonder? Or has it some other reason for stalling?
If Mr. Gardiner had used the international situation and the defence program as a pretext for delay-

At this late date in the session, Mr. Chairman, I shall not carry out my threat to make a forty-minute speech giving my own ideas, although I assure the hon. member that on this subject I could speak for forty minutes with the greatest of ease. I shall say this, and it is not a quotation. We understand well enough that this is a long-term project. We do not want this government to enter into a national proposition, as this certainly is, without due care and consideration. But I do violently object to having this thing made into an election political football. I do violently
