object to being promised the project at every election, and then finding after the election is over that the government is pussyfooting and delaying getting on with the project. That is what I wanted to say.
I am going to make the prediction, Mr. Chairman, that before the next election comes there will be lots of dam building machinery down around the project. If the machinery is not there, then the minister will be there himself telling us once more that if the Liberal government is just returned to power in this country we will have the dam project in no time.
Would it not be wise for the minister to give us that outline of the project which he promised?
I might say, Mr. Chairman-

Before the minister
speaks, I have only a few brief remarks I should like to make. I do not want to repeat anything that has been said. I believe the situation is that the commission has not reported as yet; therefore I may not be as critical as I might otherwise be. I should like to ask the minister to do what he can to get an early report. Certainly the postponements that have taken place and the excuses that have been made in the last two years for not proceeding with the work have aroused a feeling of antagonism which was clearly evident at the meeting which took place last week at Outlook, to which the hon.. member referred.
One interesting feature that was brought to the attention of the gathering there was a preview of the irrigation project which was given to those who were in attendance at this function, numbering some 243. I read from the Regina Leader-Post, in which it is stated:
A preview of what south central Saskatchewan may expect in the way of crops and crop yields when irrigation replaces dry farming here was given to about 100 visitors who toured the P.F.R.A. pre-development farm at Outlook Friday.
Dr. Thomson told delegates that it was a 1948 S.R.D.A. resolution that had been responsible for the government setting up the pre-development farm two years ago. And since that time the farm had been experimenting with a variety of crops to determine their suitability under irrigation.
The farm-160 acres-had 60 acres under the sprinkler system and the balance under gravity irrigation.
From the experiments that have taken place there, some indication was given as to the extent to which -crop rotation could be proceeded with in that area. I think that was a most commendable piece of work on the part of the department and one that deserves the support of all the members, particularly from Saskatchewan. We realize that if this
[Mr. Knight.l
project is proceeded with it will mean irrigation being made available to some 500,000 acres or even more, in an area that throughout the years has suffered, from recurrent drought. Certainly it is rather difficult to understand why it became necessary to set up a commission to review the conclusions arrived at by the engineers of the Department of Agriculture and those connected with the P.F.R.A. Those engineers know conditions in Saskatchewan. Their experience is practical; and more than three years ago, if my recollection is correct, they determined that this scheme was practicable and that in addition to the irrigation possibilities and the probable improvement of production- in that area, it would also provide a power development for Saskatchewan. Without such a development Saskatchewan could never hope to achieve a basis of industrial equality with the other provinces.
I think, in addition to the irrigation possibilities, the development of power there will be of material advantage in placing that province in a position to take advantage of some of its industrial potentialities. When you realize all the hundreds of millions of dollars being spent on defence, and the small drop as it were, finding its way into Saskatchewan, -and that it would be otherwise if there were a power development, the necessity for something being done immediately in this connection is apparent.
The commission was set up composed- of Dr. Hogg and two other distinguished gentlemen, Dr. Widtsoe and the president of the Calgary Power whose name I forget. That commission has had its ups and downs, and one chairman was ill. But the postponement and the procrastination that have taken place in connection with this matter are difficult to understand. The minister himself stated more than two years ago that this scheme had been found to be practicable and that there was no doubt as to the potentialities that were apparent in the province provided the plan was gone ahead with. For some reason-apparently the other ministers in the cabinet do not share the view taken by the Minister of Agriculture-the commission is set up. The commission now has been sitting for several months, or at least it has been in the process of sitting from time to time; yet we are apparently no nearer a solution to this problem than we were last year.
I feel that the delegates to this association were justified in the conclusions to which they came and to which the hon. member for Saskatoon made reference. He quoted from the resolutions or the general attitude adopted by the membership of this association; and no one can criticize them for taking the

stand they now take, namely that the time has come-to use the words of Dr. Tufts-to take off the kid gloves and let Ottawa know that Saskatchewan is fed up with delays and excuses.
With all the hundreds of millions and billions of dollars being spent for defence and with this being a project that is needed in Saskatchewan, one that will be self-liquidating, one that in the years to come will pay dividends far in excess of any cost, the latest delay or the latest reason for delay, namely that engineers have to be called in to ascertain what the cost would now be, is scarcely in keeping with the kind of action the people of Saskatchewan have the right to expect.
I look back to 1944 and just prior to the election of 1945. Many teams and outfits started to work there. They were in the investigatory stage. After the election we passed to an expenditure of about $1 million a year; but since 1949 there has been nothing but delay. Small expenditures have been made, but we in the province of Saskatchewan certainly believe that the views expressed by the association and by Dr. Tufts are representative of a viewpoint held without regard to party considerations. All we want the minister to know is that we are with him in what he has told us he is endeavouring to do, namely to get this work under way with as little delay as possible.

In reference to the position in Saskatchewan, I would point out that none of us object to bringing as much prosperity as possible to the farms of Saskatchewan. But we are paying a large sum of money in order to indemnify freight from Saskatchewan to the various sources where animals are fed in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and elsewhere. I want to say that I have a brother in Saskatoon who is feeding 500 cattle. I have another brother in the province of Ontario who is also feeding cattle, either a lesser or a larger number. The one in Ontario receives the benefit of free freight on feed from Saskatchewan to Ontario and is, as it were, in competition with the other brother who, at Saskatoon, at the very source of this feed, is handling his cattle. I say the various parts of our country depend one upon the other. We must remember that a great sum of money is going out from the treasury of Canada to indemnify those who are shipping cheap feed from Saskatchewan to British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec and elsewhere in Canada.

I want to say a word on this item. If I looked at the map for the proposed new constituency of Rosetown-Big-gar, I think I could say that probably my

constituents will have a still greater interest in it than they have had previously; because if the redistribution is made in the way it seems it is going to be, Rosetown-Biggar will comprise the whole of west central Saskatchewan, and both sides of the great river; thus the irrigation project on the South Saskatchewan river will be almost entirely in the new constituency of Rosetown-Biggar. However, I do not mind that because, as a matter of fact, if this irrigation plan goes through it will irrigate one of the finest sections of Saskatchewan. Already those who have a knowledge of soils and irrigation tell me that the area to be irrigated, or at least 450,000 acres of it, is far above the average in the potential production and fertility usually associated with irrigation projects.
I have always been in favour of this plan and, like the members who have spoken, I hope it will not be delayed further. When the commission was appointed a year ago I was rather surprised at the personnel. This is essentially an irrigation project, with power important perhaps but incidental to it. Whether the development of power on the river is feasible or economic should not in any respect interfere with the carrying out of what is essentially an irrigation project, power being I repeat relatively incidental. I was therefore greatly surprised when only one outstanding irrigation man was included on that commission of three, namely Dr. Widtsoe of Salt Lake City who, as we know, is one of the outstanding authorities on this continent with respect to irrigation projects. The other two gentlemen, Dr. Hogg, the former chairman of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, and Mr. Gaherty, president of the Calgary Power Limited, were both primarily interested in electric development. When a project was primarily for irrigation and power Was merely incidental thereto, and it was only in the power aspect that any doubt has been cast upon the project, as far as I know, I found it difficult to understand why a commission of that type should have been set up. I should have liked to have seen the commission weighted the other way, namely with two outstanding irrigation men and one power man.
This project has been a long time in prospect. As a matter of fact it was discussed a long time before 1944. I remember distinctly moving a resolution in this house in 1947.

Yes, 1937. I remember moving a resolution in this house dealing

Supply-Agriculture
with irrigation projects in Saskatchewan-it was during the drought period-and spending quite a little time on the possibility of using the rivers which flow through Saskatchewan and more particularly, of course, the southern branch of the great Saskatchewan river which we know as the South Saskatchewan. This project was in prospect long before that time, of course. There was the Pearce report and the Pearce plan. I have forgotten what year that was but it was in the early part of this century; I believe it was in 1922. I remember the hon. member for Acadia discussing that plan and the irrigation possibilities of these western rivers.
The government may take the attitude that there is not the pressing need for it at the present time because there is plenty of water on the prairies. As a matter of fact I have never seen as much water in the 43 years I have been on the prairies as we have there at the present time. But we all know that the history of the prairies proves that is only a temporary condition, and at some time or other that water will go and the prairies will be subject to dry conditions again.
That has been the history of the prairies; it is to be found recorded in the soils, and if you look at the rings of the trees you can find it written in the trees that grow in the prairie regions. I say to hon. members who are not from the prairies that in my opinion this is one of the great insurance projects , for all Canada and the economy of all Canada. By the time this dam is built and the irrigation ditches finished and the country irrigated we may once again enter upon a period of dry years. We do not know, but that has been the history of our prairie country.
I am most anxious to see this project proceeded with. I know it is a considerable project; I know the government and the country must be satisfied that the dam can be built; that the foundations must be such as to carry the dam and keep back the water and see that no seepage underneath will undermine the dam. 1 say that because I wondered why the minister introduced a doubt in Saskatoon quite recently: warning that in the event of the dam going out the city of Saskatoon would be the one city which would be wiped out.
I did not introduce that recently. My hon. friend sitting behind the hon. member is able to tell him that I have been saying that for many years.

Well, this was the first time I had seen it played up to the extent it was played up on June 9 in the city of

Saskatoon. It almost looked as though the minister were trying to frighten the people away from the project. That was the way it looked to me when I read the newspaper report. But I am convinced of this, that the engineers who have surveyed the dam site know full well that a dam can be built with perfect safety and with security for the city of Saskatoon, and I have been satisfied that that could be done for a number of years now.
I certainly would like to see the report of the commission tabled in the house so we might know exactly what they had to say about it. I know that one of the reasons for the delay in the report is the illness of Dr. Hogg. Dr. Hogg I was sorry to learn has been apparently in ill health for a very considerable time. If I may say this with all due respect to Dr. Hogg- I know the difficulties the government would have in adopting the suggestion, but I am going to make it-in the interest of this project, if Dr. Hogg is to continue in ill health, extending over a long period of time, he should hand his resignation to the government in order that he might be replaced by someone who could carry forward this investigation, because delay is holding up the development of a whole section of Canada, in this prairie region, a region which has great potential production. Nothing else is holding it up.
I know it was said in this house, and I was rather surprised-I am not blaming the Prime Minister because the answer to the question of the hon. member for Kindersley would have been provided by his advisers- sometime in March that the delay was owing to the fact that the Saskatchewan government had not submitted a brief. Well, I happened to know from the secretary of the commission at that time, whom I met casually a short time before, that it had been agreed with the commission that no further brief was necessary, and that until the public hearings, if they ever were held, were undertaken, nothing more was expected from the government of Saskatchewan. I knew that at the time. I say I knew that from the secretary of the commission, and obtained the information in a casual conversation. Therefore I say, Mr. Chairman, that these excuses will no longer hold water. What we want is the dam to hold water, and I have no doubt that if the dam were built, it would hold water. As the hon. member for -is it still Lake Centre?
Yes.

As the hon. member for Lake Centre indicated a few moments ago the demonstration that has been prepared

at Outlook has illustrated what irrigation will mean to the area. Incidentally, the town of Outlook was across the river from the rest of my constituency in 1935; and I always wondered why it was included in Rosetown-Biggar at that time. Well, now it will be right in the very centre of the constituency because of the manner in which it is to be enlarged, so I shall have a beautiful garden in the middle of my constituency to demonstrate the feasibility and desirability of the South Saskatchewan river scheme.
When the minister rises I hope he will answer the request of the hon. member for Lethbridge and give us the information requested; but most of all I hope he will be able to tell us that the final report is about to be made, and that when the report is made-I hope it will be a satisfactory one- the appropriations will be made to proceed with this project.
It is quite true, as the hon. member for Lake Centre said a few moments ago, that we can find billions of dollars when we have to, and we have to find billions of dollars, for defence. I am not criticizing that; but when we have to find it for defence we can find those billions of dollars. Here is a plan which is a defence plan too.
And self-liquidating.

And self-liquidating, not a wasting expense as defence expenditures usually are. It is a self-liquidating defence plan, a defence plan against what? Against possible drought and impoverishment of a large section of the country, and needed in the production of quantities of food-and food may in the long run be the very best means of defence the democratic world can find in this period of the world's history. Therefore I want to join not only with members of the Conservative party and my own party and the Social Credit party, but I am quite sure with many members of the minister's own party, in urging the immediate undertaking of this great irrigation project in the province of Saskatchewan.

Before the minister speaks on this I wish to add some comments to what has been said about this project. I do so because I think it would be unfortunate if the impression were unintentionally conveyed that this is something of interest only to the people of Saskatchewan. It is something of very great interest to the people of the whole of Canada.
One of the subjects that have been causing hon. members some concern in the past few days is the impact of the reduction of population in the province of Saskatchewan. That has been partly the result of changing
Supply-Agriculture
methods of agricultural production with the effect of greater mechanization, but also it has been very largely the result of the failure to deal with this problem years ago. Look at the areas where there has been a heavy reduction of population, and you will find some of the greatest reductions in the very area that would have been served by this irrigation project if it had been undertaken some fifteen years ago when it was first proposed and first regarded as a satisfactory project.
When I say this is something of concern to every member of the house and to every Canadian, I do so at a time when members are asked to regard the St. Lawrence deep waterway as a subject of interest to every Canadian. Those who live in the area where the most immediate benefit from the St. Lawrence deep waterway and power project would be felt ask the people from other parts of Canada to regard this as a national project, and not one that would be of interest only to that part of the country which will benefit most directly from the result of what is done in the area, at very considerable cost to all Canadian taxpayers.
May I say that the St. Lawrence project has been regarded in that light. I would like to see every member of the House of Commons regard the South Saskatchewan development in the same light, as a development which should be undertaken not only in the interests of Saskatchewan but in the interests of Canada as a whole, and as part of the general development of this country.
Having said that I do wish to emphasize the fact that this is naturally a subject of very great concern to the people of Saskatchewan living in that area. I am however impressed with the difference in the approach to this subject as compared with the approach to the St. Lawrence deep waterway. This government has committed itself irrevocably to the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway and the development of the power projects associated with it, although there are still uncertainties as to all the details connected with the carrying out of that immense project at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. The government expressed no unwillingness to commit the Canadian taxpayers as a whole to this project, though it was clear that there were certain details still to be worked out. They recognized the principle as sound, and the government and members of the house have committed themselves to the fulfilment of the project, though certain details must still be carried out.

To the tune of $800 million.

I believe that long ago the House of Commons should have been given the opportunity to express its acceptance of the principle of this project, and should then have said to the engineers, "This job needs to be done." I am not saying that any project of this kind should be undertaken recklessly or without adequate consideration. We have had adequate engineering advice to the effect that this is a sound project.
First of all, there is clear evidence to be seen by anyone who visits that part of the country that this irrigation area, now almost a dust-bowl, can become one of the most productive agricultural areas in Canada. It has already been pointed out that near Outlook there is an experimental area which has been irrigated. In that area one will see as rich production and as fresh growth as can be seen anywhere in Canada. In that area one can see evidence of what irrigation of this kind would mean.
I do not want to take issue with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in anything he has said, because I agree with the general views he expressed. But there is one feature of this project that I believe requires emphasis. While the first concern, naturally, is the restoration of the productive capacity of tlm soil in that area, and to that extent irrigation is the primary consideration, it should be remembered that it will only be with electrical power that the irrigation can be carried out. It will take a very substantial part-perhaps a third or a half-of the primary electrical power to carry out the full project, and to provide the power for the pumping stations which will be needed to carry the water to the most distant points. Of course I admit that other types of power could be employed, fuel oil or gas, perhaps. But the project I have heard discussed when I have visited that area, and the plans I have seen, have been based upon the use of electrical power for the irrigation project itself.
I do not wish to be misunderstood; what I meant was that primarily this is an irrigation project.

As I said, I am not taking issue with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I was simply pointing out that the development of power is an essential feature of this development, unless fuel oil or natural gas were employed for that purpose. Conceivably at some time that might be a desirable development; but in the first instance it would seem -that electrical energy is the most economical method of carrying out this development.

I do not claim expert knowledge beyond the fact that I have been associated with some decisions connected with power development of one kind or another, but I think it is safe to say that there are few places in Canada today where construction would be easier in connection with the erection of a dam for holding back the water for purposes of irrigation, and also for the provision of the necessary headwaters for the production of power in that area.
As I understand it, the engineers have agreed on a site where a dam can be constructed satisfactorily. There are no great rock cuts; there are no diversions of rivers or anything of that kind involved. It is a straight filling proposition between even, river banks, one of the simplest engineering projects that could be imagined for the purpose of carrying out this great undertaking.
I am convinced that those who have been associated with the advancement of this project over the years have been working on a perfectly sound basis. Dr. Tufts, at Outlook, who has headed the local organization, has at all times spoken with moderation in regard to the project, and has at all times, along with those associated with him, sought to rely upon expert engineering reports in the proposals he has made. I mention this now because, while the effect of anything that is done will naturally be felt immediately by the people of Saskatchewan, I think all of us in the house should regard it as the responsibility of Canada as a whole, and we should ask the government to commit itself without further delay to the decision to proceed with this project. There is plenty of evidence that it is a sound project, and the engineering details can be worked out by those who are entrusted with the fulfilment of the undertaking.

The government will not commit itself to this project until there has been a report that it is sound economically, and that it would be a proper investment of the money of the people of Canada. But if that is established-and I hope it will be established, as I have said before in the house-I think it is a project that is not merely in the interests of Saskatchewan but is in the interests of the Canadian nation.
There have been many engineering reports that it is physically possible to build a dam there that will stand, although it is a very high earthen embankment that is required, and not just as simple as the leader of the opposition, in his remarks, would represent it to be. There have been engineering reports upon it, and it has been established to our

satisfaction that it is physically possible as an engineering proposition.
There remains the question as to whether that would be a proper capital investment for the people to make in view of its cost and the benefits to be derived from it. With respect to the production of electrical power there is still a question as to whether it could be produced more economically from the water that would thus be stored up or from low-grade fuels which are abundant in that part of Canada. That is a question upon which the leader of the opposition may have an opinion based upon data available to him; I have not. I have seen the reports made by those who hold conflicting views upon it, and I am not in position to form an opinion as to whether it would be better to produce hydro power or to use low-grade fuel to produce the same amount of electricity.
There is a considerable area that it is considered would be made much more productive. I do not remember the exact acreage, but I know it is substantial. It would represent a capital cost of many dollars per acre to provide the necessary reservoir. But I do not think that should frighten us. When our ancestors went ahead and built a railroad across the continent from one ocean to the other there were those who said that it would never earn its axle grease, but I think events have proved that that kind of investment and the spirit of adventure that made that investment possible was the kind of thing that has brought Canada to the position we enjoy today.
Hon. gentlemen will remember that in the speech from the throne in the session preceding this session three projects of national importance were put forward and lumped together. There was the St. Lawrence seaway project which will run into a large sum of money. A major portion of the hundreds of millions required for that project will be devoted to the production of hydroelectric power. I have been informed by reliable sources that the production of that power will mean to the people of Ontario, over and above the interest and amortization and the cost of operation of the hydroelectric plant, a saving of at least $25 million per year when compared with the cost of producing power by any other means that would be available.
The other half of the hydroelectric development will be paid for and taken care of by the agency to be appointed by the government of the United States to develop its share of the waterpower available. The second scheme put forward at the same time was the Canso causeway. Our population has increased two and a half times in the last fifty years; from five and a quarter millions it has become 14 millions and is increasing now as rapidly as at any time this century. This means that at

Mr. Chairman, I think this has been the finest debate I have heard in this house on the subject of the South Saskatchewan river project. I was delighted to hear both the leader of the opposition and the right hon. Prime Minister express views on the subject tonight. It seems to me that in their cogent statements can be found great comfort and hope for the people, not only of Saskatchewan but of all Canada, who have been wanting to see this great project completed at the earliest possible time. I want merely to stand as a sort of second witness to some of the things that have been said- not, Mr. Chairman, to take time unnecessarily but because I believe what I have to say will be quite important and quite pertinent to the subject under discussion.
I am glad to see the Minister of Finance here tonight because some of the things I have to say are going to be directed right to him. He is the main person on the treasury board and I want him to pay particular attention to one or two things I shall have to say.
We in the province of Alberta, Mr. Chairman, have proved the value of irrigation in the west. We started in that province as far back as 1889, and I have witnessed in my lifetime what can happen to a farm on that very dry Palliser triangle when water is applied to it. I have also witnessed-and this bears out what the Prime Minister said a moment ago-the development of a small scheme in southern Alberta where the Alberta Railway and Irrigation Company in 1889 built a project at its own expense, settled the area, colonized, developed and eventually practically gave the whole project to the settlers, because they found that settlement and development was contributing so much to their traffic and freight income that it was possible for them to do that very thing.

Mr. Chairman,
Brigham Young was a hundred years too soon.

You were a hundred years too late. My hon. friend from Cariboo must be feeling pretty good again tonight, but I can appreciate that and I can shake off his remarks.
I also saw the Canadian Pacific Railway develop a project in central Alberta, colonize it and eventually hand it over to the settlers for the sum of $1; and in addition they gave those settlers a considerable sum of money- if I remember correctly it was pushing up to half a million dollars in cash-to help them, finance the works and so on that in time [DOT]were expected to be completed. If they could do that it simply evidences what the Prime Minister has already said; that the cost of development of these great national projects to strengthen our production can be reaped many times over in the revenue received by the railways, by the federal treasury, and in a good many instances by business concerns.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as I said we have demonstrated all that. Although the province of Alberta has had to carry some pretty heavy costs in the past that was due to the fact that up until comparatively recently there was no such thing as an agreement between the provinces and the dominion for sharing the costs of irrigation. In Alberta the Lethbridge northern irrigation district was formed in 1918 or 1919, if I remember correctly. I recall only too well the history of that project and what it involved. As I remember, it cost them $50 an acre of irrigable land to build the project. That cost was presumed to have been attached to the land itself and the settlers were supposed to be able to pay the capital cost and to make out in time from the profit.
Is that the E.I.D.?

No, that is up in central Alberta. I am speaking about the Lethbridge northern irrigation district in and around the city of Lethbridge.
The government of the province of Alberta had to guarantee the bonds of the Lethbridge northern irrigation district to the full extent of the $50 an acre cost. It was about 1919 or 1920 that they got under way. The bonds were sold under a guarantee of the province; but, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the fact that the land was good, that the system itself was good, that the works were excellent and that the farmers put on the land learned quickly how to use the water, it took a good many years before that project began to return sufficient to the settlers that they could pay off the indebtedness; and then not until the province of Alberta finally took over and assumed the full cost of the project

they had guaranteed. Since that date they have been paying interest on the bonds and paying off the bonds-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
When did this land come into production and what was the state of prices at that time? Did they come in at a bad year?

No, the land began to come under ditches in about 1925, if I remember correctly, and that would be in the heyday of the buoyancy of this country. It is the Lethbridge northern I am speaking about; and at that time it was presumed that the total value of the land, including the $50 per acre cost of putting the water on it, would be approximately $100 to $125 an acre. Well, the settlers were presumed to be able to pay the $100 to $125 an acre, but it was demonstrated for at least some years in the hard times that they could not do so. If I remember correctly, about 1933 or 1934 it was necessary for the government of the province to assume the indebtedness against the project and start paying the interest on the bonds themselves.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that project will cost the government of the province of Alberta, before they are finished with it, $11 to $12 million, I believe; but it has proved its value many times over and the province does not regret the dollars they have spent on it. The project has become a wealthy project that is producing in tremendous abundance and does contribute immeasurably to the stability of our province. The Picture Butte sugar refinery is built on that project and is producing something like 100 million pounds of sugar per year. That in itself, together with the auxiliary industries like the feed industry in that area, makes it a very important project indeed.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am grateful for this. Eventually the federal government came to realize that these irrigation schemes were national development projects, and they are now recognizing that fact more than ever. The Prime Minister informed us of that tonight when speaking of the South Saskatchewan dam. But it has taken some years to come to that point of view, and now in the province of Alberta we have one or two fairly large schemes under way that are based upon a contribution of about 50 per cent federal and 50 per cent provincial money. That is all to the good and we in Alberta are not complaining about it. In fact 55704-249

we are very thankful that the Minister of Agriculture and his associates in the dominion government have seen fit to value those projects highly enough that they will contribute 50 per cent of the cost.
There is just one thing I would like to say by way of encouragement to my friends in Saskatchewan. Having said that, Mr. Chairman, let me emphasize this important point. I suspect that one of the things that may-I am not saying will but may-hold that project up or delay it, and I am speaking now of the Outlook project for irrigation and power production in Saskatchewan, is that the federal government may insist on an agreement with the province of Saskatchewan on a fifty-fifty cost basis.
While it is perfectly true that in Alberta we have been making out quite successfully under a fifty-fifty arrangement on the Lethbridge southeastern and other projects, we feel that this project in Saskatchewan is not only a national development project but in some respects, Mr. Chairman, a reimbursement project. When I say that I mean that for a good many years Saskatchewan has been shouldering a heavy burden of cost as a consequence of dominion settlement policies prior to 1931 when the resources were handed over to that province. The people of the province were carrying the burden even before it was organized in 1905. I think the hon. member for Lethbridge made that quite clear when he described the Palliser triangle settlement and the problems involved as a consequence of that rather blind policy, as it seemed to me under the circumstances.
I want to declare my conviction that Saskatchewan should not be required to bear half of the cost of the Outlook project as is required under national development projects, some of which we have in Alberta and some of which are elsewhere in this country. I say that for this reason. The Saskatchewan economy simply cannot under present circumstances carry that 50 per cent of the cost. I am convinced of that. Let us look at three important reasons why I say

that. In the first place, remember that Saskatchewan has largely a prairie wheat economy, even today. The second reason Saskatchewan could not be expected to carry 50 per cent of the cost of that tremendous scheme, which I understand will be something like $100 million, is that the province is already carrying tremendous burdens by reason of its geography, population and so on. Let me give you one or two illustrations that help explain what I mean. In Saskatchewan today the number of miles of highway the province has to build and maintain per thousand of population is 169. Do you live in Saskatchewan?

The miles of telephone wire that have to be maintained per telephone unit in that province is 5 22/100, as compared with Ontario's 4 31/100. The acreage for the province of Saskatchewan compared to the population is 60-4, while in the province of Ontario it is only 6 * 6. Those figures tell a story; they indicate something

of the terrific burden the people of that province do have to carry financially. I could go on and give innumerable examples of the burdens the province has to carry.
Let me point out, Mr. Chairman, a third reason why I feel Saskatchewan cannot possibly be expected to pay 50 per cent of the total cost of the project. There is a comparatively small population in this very large area, and they have a total budget of only $66 million a year to carry all the services for their people, pay interest on their debt, the amortization of the debt itself, and build public works and other projects. Let us not forget this. I have given reasons, Mr. Chairman, why I feel that when it comes time to make a deal with Saskatchewan we ought to take into consideration those facts I have presented. I believe we should not feel that we have established a pattern by asking the province of Saskatchewan to pay 50 per cent of the total cost of the irrigation projects in that province. I think perhaps we have been fortunate in being in a position to carry our 50 per cent. I do not believe we should impose that sort of agreement on the province of Saskatchewan.
I do not want to take too much of the time of the committee tonight, but I did want to present that case because I am genuinely interested in the extension and development of irrigation in this country. I want to see Saskatchewan enjoy the benefits we have enjoyed in Alberta for years, but for which we have paid rather dearly.

What I agreed to do the other day was give a short outline of what we call the larger irrigation projects in western Canada.
As to that meeting in Washington the other day, has a report been issued? Is it available?
I am coming back to that matter in a minute or two. First, I want to cover the four projects.
All right.

What I agreed to do the other day was give a short outline of what we call the large irrigation projects in western Canada. About nine or ten years ago we started out to make a systematic survey of the water projects in the west, and more particularly those associated with the Saskatchewan river system. Out of those investigations we developed four projects, three of them in Alberta and one in Saskatchewan. The one in Alberta that has had the greatest amount of publicity has been the St. Mary dam project. Behind the St. Mary dam is another one known as the Waterton dam which is still to be constructed and which we must construct if we are going to have made available a sufficient amount of water for the other projects which are being discussed from time to time in western Canada. We have already undertaken that that is a part of that project, when completed, and is associated with the international relationships in connection with water.
The St. Mary dam. itself has been built at a cost of about $12 million, in round figures, with connecting ditches between that and the storages all through the area that is to be irrigated. The province has undertaken to arrange for the expenditure of a similar amount of money to complete the ditches and storages throughout what is known as the irrigation district. That irrigation district extends roughly from the neighbourhood of Taber, I think, on toward Medicine Hat. The result of the operations, when completed, will be that some 500,000 acres of land, or something approaching that figure, will be under irrigation.
One has only to travel from Medicine Hat to Lethbridge, either by air or by car, at this time of year in order to realize just what

that irrigation has meant up until now. One passes over a road allowance near Taber, and one would think that one is in an entirely different country or in an entirely different area. The growth is great. The industry in the towns and villages is far more than comparable with that which can be found in some of the areas farther south where rainfall makes possible similar development. If one flies over it, one is moved to the conclusion that at least three times as many people live where the irrigation is as live where there is no irrigation.
That is right.

To fly over the farm homes and villages in that area makes one feel that even the one-third of the people who are in the less densely populated area are too many for that area. They are not living under conditions which people should be living under. Immediately water is put on the land these people benefit to an extent that one who has not seen it can scarcely realize. I only want to say that much with regard to the matter in order to emphasize the fact that it is a good thing for a country to be irrigated, irrespective of what the cost may be.
As has been suggested, the general cost of getting that land under water is something over $50. It is about $54. It stands to reason that the farmer who is going to live on the land is not in a position to pay that cost in addition to paying for the land, and for those other costs of operation, and paying taxation in connection with the building of roads and all that kind of thing. He is just not in a position to do that. It has therefore been thought that some authority ought to take some responsibility for it.
Some years ago-back in 1941 or 1942, I think it was-we had a report made. It was called the Meek report. That report was compiled by five or six individuals, some of whom were engineers. A few moments ago the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested that he was somewhat at a loss to know why the men who had been selected to be on the committee which is now investigating should have been chosen. This is all I am going to say about it at the moment; I will say a little more about it later.
One of the men, namely Mr. Gaherty, was on that committee. He was one of those who reported in favour of the irrigation schemes that are being developed or that are being talked about out in western Canada. He therefore has had experience which is of some value. There is not much need for discussing the St. Mary project any further than that. We have spent about $12 million

on it. The province is in the process of spending about an equal amount in order to get water on the land that is now being irrigated through the building of the St. Mary dam, and it will be necessary to spend another few million in order to put in the Waterton dam in order to provide further waters for utilization through that system.
The next system that has been under consideration is the Bow river. That is an old project which was started through the investment of British capital. Some $13 million were spent by a British company in order to start irrigation in that country. They started out with the idea that they could make the farmers pay all the money back. At one time they thought they could get them to pay $75 an acre. They realized before very long that they were just driving people off the land by attempting that. Later on they reduced it to the neighbourhood of $50 an acre, and still it was too much. Finally they got it down to $27 an acre, and I think they are still asking them to pay $27.
My opinion is that prior to the war it was impossible for these farmers to pay $27 an acre. None of them was clearing his land. But the last time I was there and discussed it with them about half had their land absolutely clear as a result of the fact that we have had high prices and high production during the war period and since. But even when one went there three or four years ago and took a look at that area one was disappointed. When one compared that with what one would see down around Taber and in that country one was disappointed, because the surroundings of the homes were not very much better than they were out on the dry lands of the prairie country. The reason was that too much was being taken out of the persons who were living on the land, and they were not able to maintain their homes in the way they should be maintained.
To make a long story short, the government decided to buy out the interest of those who had been in the project before. We paid $2,225,000 for it, and we are improving the ditches. We are now developing or levelling the lands and making it possible for people to settle on some 40,000 acres more in that area; and we are bringing the people to settle on it from the lands that we are developing into pastures elsewhere, in order to take them off dry land.
That development is going along and I do not need to say any more about it than that we had financial arrangement from the beginning with the Alberta governments with whom we started to make agreements; and it is written into our correspondence in connection with those agreements that we would

develop first the St. Mary project; that is, we would put in the storages in the St. Mary project; that we would adopt the same method and develop the Canada Land and Irrigation or the Bow river project. I should say before leaving that, that associated with it are some lands that the province is developing, as well as the lands which we are developing, and the number of people who will be served by that is much greater than the number we are placing on the land.
Well, then, there is the third project in the province of Alberta that has been fully investigated, and that we would be in a position to proceed with at any time if it were once determined that those projects are going to be gone ahead with; that is the Red Deer project. The lands that we are concerned with are largely around Hanna. Some 400,000 or 500,000 acres of land in that project could be irrigated. I am not going into the details as to how it could be done. Dams would have to be built; siphons would have to be built; ditches would have to be dug in order to take the water down closer to the area, and the costs could be on about the same basis as they are down in the St. Mary area. The costs there work out at about 50 per cent by the province and about 50 per cent by the federal government if we once undertake to go ahead with the project in co-operation with the provincial government. The costs of that project would be considerably less than the St. Mary dam project.
There is one difficulty about the discussion of the question recently, and it is that some of those who have been discussing the matter, and some of those who have been placing it before this commission that has been sitting have again started to discuss the old Pearce scheme of years ago. That was a scheme I heard discussed when I became a minister seventeen years ago and went to Hanna. At a public meeting that was being held that scheme was still being talked about. That scheme envisages the digging of an open ditch from Hanna to Saskatoon, about 500 miles long, through country much of which is sandy, where there would be great leakage of water from the ditch out over the areas, and where the costs of getting the water down there would be very great.
To make a long story short, at that meeting the engineers who were present convinced themselves and convinced everyone there that we should drop the idea of the Pearce scheme, of this ditch running all the way to Saskatoon and irrigating not only 500,000 acres of land at Hanna but some million acres of land between that and Saskatoon, including the lands now spoken of in connection with the

South Saskatchewan river. I want to say that so far as I am concerned, and so far as the people of western Canada are concerned, I think we were convinced long ago that that was not a project which was feasible. It has been suggested that we have the wrong type of individuals on the commission that is investigating the whole matter. I am convinced that the engineers we have developed over the years in connection with this kind of work are the best engineers in Canada at least, the best engineers that can be found anywhere to deal with water development. As a matter of fact I think they are the only engineers that have the ability, because of their experience and training, either to examine into or to give a final answer to the question whether a dam can be built and what the results of building a dam would be in so far as that area is concerned. But we were not satisfied to rely upon these men, and so we went down to the United States

and got three of the best engineers that are known, one of them being Mr. Ferguson, who was associated with the building of large dams down there, and associated with the army throughout the war. I think the leader of the opposition will be the first to agree that when he went out west at first, after having been chosen leader of his party, he stated to the press that he was not informed with regard to the matter, and on that occasion he did not discuss it very freely. went back later and became better acquainted with it, and on that occasion discussed it more freely.

But at the same time, being at the head of the government of the country, and the one who must take the responsibility eventually for any expenditures made, he has taken the position that we ought to remove any doubt with regard to the matter, if it can possibly be removed, before undertaking the project itself. I have not been inclined to hurry the Prime Minister or to hurry other members of the government, as they will agree. I have been inclined to say that I am still convinced myself that the project is a good project; I am still convinced that it would be one of the most helpful things for the people of Saskatchewan that could possibly be done by this government; and, through the people of Saskatchewan, also most helpful to the people of all Canada.
At the same time I must admit that what the Prime Minister said tonight was that some question had been raised as to whether the most feasible way of developing power is by developing it from water. That idea was not raised by our engineers; it was raised by an engineer engaged by the provincial government; and let me say that I am not criticizing them for engaging him. We get all the information we can in all these matters. Nevertheless he did raise the question whether the power could not be developed more cheaply from coal than through the damming up of these waters. He even raised the question of gas, too, which arose from the fact that gas was found in the neighbourhood of Rosetown, and it was thought possible even at the time he was making his report that that might be a possibility. Gas has been found there, and it has been suggested that it might be used for the purpose.

But what those of us who are in favour of the dam have been saying persistently and consistently is that it does not make any difference how you get the power; it does not make any difference whether you have power from the water that is there, or whether you have power from coal, or whether you have power from gas, or whether you get all the power you require from oil. The fact is that the power is not any good in that country unless you get water first. There has to be water before there can be any industry. It does not matter whether there is power or not. You cannot put industry in an area where there is no possibility of having a water supply. That would be not only for the purpose of developing power, but for the purpose of supplying water for all the uses to which water would be put in industry.
So we have always contended that the lake must be there. After that we have said power can be developed from that lake, and that the development of the power itself could be charged up to the land that is going to be irrigated. What the report actually does say is that if you charge the proper amount of the cost up to the power that will be developed, then the cost that will be charged against the irrigated land is almost exactly the same as the cost that is charged up in the Lethbridge area, and that is about $54 an acre. So the contention is that the dam should be built and the power should be developed. One of the reasons for having on the committee men who are associated with the development of power is to satisfy everyone that that is a possibility.
When you have satisfied them that it is a possibility, there is still one other question. Is the development of industry which would be associated with the development of power and the finding of gas, and everything else associated with it that is made possible by having a lake in the middle of the area, something that is worth while for the people of this country? I must say that is one feature which the Prime Minister emphasized tonight. He hoped the result of the investigation would be such that we could all come to the conclusion that that is a fact, that the putting of a dam there and the making of a lake 145 miles long and 180 feet deep in the middle of an area short of water practically all the year round, and one year after the other, would be helpful to the whole of the Dominion of Canada. Once convinced of that, then he has suggested to us that there would not be any question, no matter what government is in power, as to whether that project would be proceeded with.
Supply-Agriculture
So I say the time has been well taken, first by the hon. member for Lethbridge bringing up the question at the beginning of the debate and, secondly, through the discussion we have had tonight. I think the time has been well taken, too, in having the question so carefully looked into. I am not sure that I want to hurry the commissioners; I am not sure what they would say if they were hurried too much. I want the commissioners before they report to have all the facts in front of them and to have the views of people right across Canada as to what they think about it. To hear men talking as they have talked here tonight, saying that other parts of Canada are just as much concerned with having this dam built as we in Saskatchewan, is worth all the waiting anyone has done. The more they keep on saying it, the better it will be. I remember when Mr. MacNicol used to sit over there. He never let a session go by without hammering into all of us that the most important thing to do in so far as the west was concerned was to utilize every drop of water that could be obtained in this country. It is nice to know that after he has gone there are others who are taking up the cudgels and saying the same thing.
Some suggestion was made in the editorial read a while ago that I may have said in Saskatoon that the reason we have delayed is the expenditures upon defence. The reason I did not say that was that I did not think it was true. That is not the reason there was delay. No one has ever said to me that is the reason why there was delay in connection with this. The suggestion has been that we want to be absolutely certain, first that the dam could be put there and kept there, which I think is pretty clearly established now; and second, that when it was put there the water would be utilized for irrigation purposes by the farmers who were on the land in that area. When we know that situation exists we will hope the project will be a good thing for all Canada.
Something has been said with regard to what the department has done in connection with an experimental farm. There is a small quarter section farm near where the dam will be which has been demonstrating what irrigation can do. I do not place as much importance upon that as do some who have spoken. It has been known for a long time that if you can put water on the land in western Canada it will grow more than any other land I know of in the world and in a shorter period of time. If we did pump water and distribute it on the land with sprays it was more to indicate to the people the methods they will have to follow if

Supply-Agriculture
irrigation is brought in. They would then know in advance what they would have to do and be ready to go ahead immediately the project was under way. I am quite sure *the discussion which has taken place will be helpful, and I hope that what has been said tonight will give some encouragement to those who have been hoping for the completion of this project.

Mr. Chairman, I was somewhat surprised to hear the minister say that certain people in Alberta are advocating the Pearce scheme in the place of the Red Deer project. That certainly is not the desire of the people in the Hanna area.
I did not use the term "Alberta". I said some people out west. I was not thinking in terms of Alberta.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, because I would not like any confusion to arise. The people in the area around Hanna are still strongly behind the Red Deer diversion project. One reason for that is that they realize there is a great deal of opposition to the original project known as the William Pearce project which later became known as the North Saskatchewan project. As the minister has pointed out, that was a very ambitious project. It meant carrying water by canals to Saskatchewan where one million acres would have been irrigated, with half a million acres in Alberta. The cost would have been around $100 million. The project would have required the diversion of water from the North Saskatchewan river to the Red Deer river. A great deal of opposition arose to the proposal to divert that water.
When I was in Hanna several years ago I suggested that it would be better if they would adopt a modified project which would utilize the waters of the Red Deer alone. The Red Deer diversion project provides for the diverting of water from the Red Deer river by means of a canal to the Hanna area where approximately half a million acres would be irrigated. That would probably be one of the cheapest projects per acre of any in Alberta because it would cost only in the neighbourhood of $15 million and would, as I say, irrigate half a million acres.
The Alberta government are strongly behind this project. I am not going to say what perhaps has been said with regard to certain other projects, that the minister has played politics with this. During the last election he was quite frank when he spoke at Hanna. He told them that regardless of what the election might bring forth it was the intention of the federal government to 
proceed with the program that had been outlined. I very much appreciate the fact that he made that clear. Since that time the federal government has spent a good deal of money on engineering details with regard to the project and also on the actual construction of dams on Berry creek and Sounding creek.
However, these dams are dependent upon the run-off of surface water. Some years water accumulates behind the dams and other years no water runs off at all. When the Red Deer diversion project is completed water will be diverted from the Red Deer river down to Berry creek and Sounding creek. In other words these lesser projects will become part and parcel of the major project. I know that in the past it has been said that the area around Hanna is submarginal, but I think what has happened in the last few years has proved that it is good land. All it needs is water. During the past two years when we have had good rains the crops have ranged from 30 to 40 bushels per acre. All the land needs is water in order to produce heavy crops.
In addition the project will flood 1,200 miles of creeks which are dry, at the present time, and will help provide for the watering of stock being carried in that area. As I say, the people in that area appreciate what has been done, but they are becoming quite anxious as to the exact intentions of the government in regard to the project. As has been mentioned, the project originated back in 1922. It has been modified several times, and people have been hoping ever since that time that they would get irrigation. All they have so far is the number of small dams on Berry creek and Sounding creek. The minister has made it clear, however, that when the St. Mary river and Bow river projects have been completed the federal government, in co-operation with the provincial government, will be ready to go ahead with the Red Deer diversion. I was glad to hear him mention these projects in that way today.
I realize some people may fear that Alberta will take more than its share of the water from the rivers that flow down from the Rocky mountains and that perhaps not sufficient water will be left for irrigation in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I understand, however, that a good deal of thought has been given to diverting rivers that flow into the Arctic to have them flow into Hudson bay. I have here a publication put out by the Alberta government entitled "Within our Borders" which reads:
Four rivers could be diverted into North Saskatchewan.

Plan of water resources office envisages diversion from Arctic watershed to compensate for irrigation drain on South Saskatchewan.
Water destined by nature to flow into the Arctic ocean may some day find itself in the Hudson's bay if a plan drafted by the water resources office is put into effect.
In a report entitled "Possible diversion from the Arctic watershed to the Saskatchewan (Hudson's bay) drainage basin," a plan is presented whereby the McLeod, Pembina, Lobstick and Wolf rivers would be diverted into the North Saskatchewan river.
Of course if that is carried out there will be no difficulty about a shortage of water, because that would provide ample water for the completion of the various projects contemplated in Alberta, and for any projects that may be contemplated in Saskatchewan or any other parts of the country. So, as I say, 1 was very glad to hear the minister mention that these projects were still being actively contemplated, and I hope it will not be too long before actual construction will be started on the Red Deer project.

I would like to ask the

Just before the item carries I should like to thank the minister for the excellent review he has given of the whole system of irrigation projects and their resulting use which will benefit the whole country. The dominion government is to be highly commended for this attack on the Palliser triangle, which is Canada's problem.
I think there might be just one point which should be emphasized finally and it is this. In my opening remarks I said and the member for Peace River said that we in Canada could not escape the fact that settlement of the Palliser triangle between 1900 and 1915 by the federal authorities then in charge of Canada incurred for Canada as a whole a responsibility to the provinces or to the administrations that were going to be under the necessity of assuming responsibility for the administra-55704-250
Supply-Agriculture
tion of the local affairs of the provinces that were to be formed from that area.
May I just review what I said the other day. It was well known from the days of Captain John Palliser in 1857 to 1860, by everyone who had a right to claim to be well informed, that the Palliser triangle area was not suitable for settlement by people intending to farm. It was acceptable only as ranching country where herds could be moved from place to place. For people who were settling down to live on the land it was absolutely unsuitable because of the altogether unpredictable nature of the rainfall in that area. Notwithstanding that, Mr. Chairman, those in parliament then advocated bringing in settlers and placing them in that area.
What was the reason for wanting settlers there? There were three reasons. The first was that the settlers would buy goods many of which would be brought in from the United States and on which they would pay duty, that duty constituting revenue for the federal government at Ottawa. Second, those people on the land would buy goods that would be produced in eastern Canada, and consequently they would provide a market for the goods of eastern Canada. Third, the bringing of those goods from eastern Canada would give the railroads business.
Although I have not the quotations before me, and I do not think it would be fitting at this late hour to read them, it is quite clear and it can easily be shown from the Hansard record of those days that those were the objects which were in the minds of the men who instituted the immigration policies under which settlers were placed in that area. Obviously then the main consideration in the minds of those men was the well-being of central Canada. I am not laying any blame on anybody, and I believe those men were wise notwithstanding the ultimate cost of the policies to the provinces concerned, but is it not about time to make up to the provinces that came to have the responsibility of governing those areas, the losses inflicted on them thereby?
There is one other thing. Really there are many things, but I do not wish to hold the house up long. The one thing is that I am very anxious that the people of Canada should get to realize from those of us who have grown up there what the facts are. Other members of the house have a right to look to us for information about that area, just as we have a right to look to the hon. member for Charlotte and the other splendid people from the maritimes for information about those provinces. If we do not tell them we are remiss in our duty.

Supply-Agriculture
So let me point this out. When the time came for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway across the nation, the obvious place to run the railway would have been up through what we call the "good" areas in the north; the bushland, where crops are almost certainly assured. That route was shorter; that route was bound to be more profitable; yet it was deemed advisable to run the C.P.R. down along the southern border where it now is, right through this Palliser triangle where there would only be a meagre opportunity for the C.P.R. to make a profitable business out of its activities. Well, what was the result? The tendency was to bring the settlement in the prairie provinces down into that Palliser triangle. Once the settlers were there, there was a responsibility for providing them with roads, schools, and all manner of social services. That responsibility had to be assumed by the provincial governments. It had to be assumed in areas where there was likely to be a crop failure any year. It was wise to run the railway down along the southern portion. Why? Because the United States railways were beginning to show a disposition to tap into Canada with their lines. Manifestly that was not in the best interests of Canada nationally. But let us remember the fact that the railroad was put there and it indirectly placed an additional financial responsibility of considerable magnitude on the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. Now when we contemplate the cost of building this dam and who is going to pay it, shall we say that we should require those provinces, and Saskatchewan in particular, to pay the full half of the cost of installing that dam? Can we look upon that as being equitable? I fail to see how we can.
There is another important matter, Mr. Chairman, that has a bearing on this whole thing. When the time came for the C.P.R. to be paid for building the railroad across Canada, paid with gifts of land, where was the land selected? It was selected in such a way that it scattered the population of Saskatchewan and Alberta all over these areas making it much more expensive to build roads to serve the people, to build telephone lines, to provide school facilities, and later much more expensive to provide health facilities. These two provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have found it necessary for example to establish travelling clinics to bring medical aid to the people in more remote areas of the provinces. All those things have constituted a tremendous disproportionate financial drain on the resources of those two provinces. Alberta by good fortune, because of the resources she has, has been placed in a better position financially than Saskatchewan. In

my judgment Saskatchewan has done the very best she could with the resources at her disposal. The Minister of Agriculture knows, better than any other person in Canada, how meagre those financial resources are compared with the tremendous responsibilities that rest upon the government of Saskatchewan. I believe the minister will bear me out in that.
I thought it well to make those three or four comments before closing, just to reinforce what the hon. member for Peace River said. I shall back the member for Peace River every inch of the way. I too do not believe that it is in any degree fair to the people of Saskatchewan to ask them to assume half the cost of building this great irrigation project.
I should like also to express appreciation to all the members who have participated in this debate. I believe that as a result of this debate it will be made easier for the minister to get the support from all over Canada which he ought to have. As a result of bringing together the support from all of Canada, we shall be able to get this great project completed at an early date and put what we might call the capstone on these irrigation projects as well. This would show our intention, as a nation, to reimburse to some extent at least the people who have settled in that area of the Palliser triangle.

47. Land protection, reclamation and development in British Columbia under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, $184,996.

On item 47 I should like to ask the minister if he would answer today a question I asked him yesterday with respect to the possibility of extending to British Columbia the prairie farm rehabilitation administration, on a basis which would make it of general application to the province. Yesterday we reviewed briefly some of the earlier discussions, and the minister said it had been in his mind for a number of years to introduce legislation which would have that effect but that for various reasons it had been postponed from time to time. I asked him yesterday if he would give us a word about the relationship between the priority that must be given to defence requirements, and the possibility of introducing legislation.
In passing the minister referred to a very similar situation tonight when he mentioned an editorial which apparently alleged that the reason for deferring the Saskatchewan river project was because of the greater priority of defence requirements. They are obviously closely related subjects, and I

wonder if the minister could give us a general word on that aspect of it.

There have been two reasons why the suggestion has been postponed from time to time. One had to do with provincial financial arrangements, and the other had to do with defence expenditures. It has not been considered wise to proceed with larger expenditure relationships with the provinces at this time. The idea has not been turned down; it has been postponed for discussion later.

There are one or two particular questions I should like to ask the minister with respect to British Columbia, just before leaving the general subject. As the minister knows, British Columbia in general has a great interest in the development within the Fraser river system of a general program of flood control, irrigation and power development. I refer again, merely in a general way, to the study which is now going forward there, and which I believe is under the over-all supervision of the Minister of Public Works. Prairie farm rehabilitation engineers are taking part in the study, so I should like to ask the minister whether it is contemplated that eventually that administration will take over the federal side of whatever project may be put forward. It seems to me it is very much the same sort of thing that is contemplated with respect to the South Saskatchewan, though if I may take the liberty of saying so I think the potentialities in that area are as great as if not greater than the other.

The proposal that is to be made is one, of course, which would have to wait for legislation such as that to which I referred. Under the constitution as it is now the responsibility is upon the province, whether it is British Columbia or any other province, for that kind of thing. Until we have legislation covering it, it is not likely that we would go into the province and take part in that development. The Department of Public Works put up the diking, and it is not the usual thing to expect to have both diking and irrigation in the same area. The Fraser river valley is fairly well watered. It is perhaps the highest rainfall area we have in any section of Canada. Talk of irrigation in that same district is rather difficult to promote here.

Evidently I have not made myself clear to the minister. The Fraser river, as he knows, goes through two entirely different areas. In the interior or dry belt area where the problem is irrigation, the river is confined to a narrow channel with large areas containing many thousands of acres 55704-250i

of bench lands anywhere from 100 to perhaps 400 feet above the actual river itself. The problem is raising the water by pumping, which requires the cheap power to which I have referred, so the water can be used to irrigate the bench lands in the upper stretches of the river and its tributaries, the Thompson and various other rivers. The farm lands or flat lands to which the minister has referred are found only in the lower reaches of the Fraser. My question is related to the study which is going forward under an organization known as the dominion-provincial board, Fraser river basin, which is surveying the whole stream and studying the possibilities of a joint power, irrigation and flood control project.
What I wanted to know was, what is the real interest of the prairie farm rehabilitation people in that work? They have engineers who are participating in that study. I have expressed the hope, and I repeat it here now, that eventually a real impetus would be given to working out a project which would provide for the three things, power development, flood control and irrigation. I am asking the minister whether there is any concrete proposal or program in his mind or the mind of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration in that regard?
